lessons.title: Exercise 17.1 — Types of Sets and Their Representation
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Set?

A well-defined collection of objects is called a set. Each object of a set is called its member (element). Sets are denoted by capital letters such as A, B, C.

Tabular Form and Set-Builder Form

In tabular form all the members are written inside curly brackets, such as A = {1, 2, 3}. In set-builder (symbolic) form the property of the members is written.

A = {x | x ∈ N ∧ x < 4} = {1, 2, 3}

Here ∈ means: is a member of. N is used for natural numbers, Z for integers, Q for rational numbers, R for real numbers, P for prime numbers and O for odd numbers.

Empty Set, Singleton Set and Equal Sets

A set which has no member is called an empty set and is denoted by ∅. A set which has only one member is called a singleton set. If two sets have exactly the same members, they are equal sets.

Finite and Infinite Sets

A set whose members can be counted and come to an end is called a finite set. A set whose members never come to an end is called an infinite set, such as the set of all prime numbers.

Subset and Equivalent Sets

If every member of A is also in B, then A is called a subset of B.

A ⊆ B

If A is a subset of B but A ≠ B, then it is a proper subset. Every set is an improper subset of itself. If two sets have the same number of members, they are equivalent sets.

Power Set

The set of all the subsets of a set is called its power set. If a set has n members, then the number of subsets in its power set is as follows.

Number of subsets = 2^n

Worked Example: Tabular Form

Example: Write the set E = {z | z ∈ R ∧ z² = 121} in tabular form.

Step 1: The condition is that z² = 121.

Step 2: 11² = 121, so z = 11 is possible.

Step 3: (-11)² = 121 also, so z = -11 is also possible.

Step 4: Both values satisfy the condition.

Step 5: So E = {-11, 11}.

Worked Example: Power Set

Example: Find the power set of A = {5, 10, 15}.

Step 1: A has 3 members, so n = 3.

Step 2: Number of subsets = 2^3 = 8.

Step 3: The subset with no member: ∅.

Step 4: One-member subsets: {5}, {10}, {15}.

Step 5: Two-member subsets: {5, 10}, {5, 15}, {10, 15}.

Step 6: The three-member subset: {5, 10, 15}.

Step 7: So P(A) = {∅, {5}, {10}, {15}, {5, 10}, {5, 15}, {10, 15}, {5, 10, 15}}.

mcqs.q: What is a set?
options: Any group of objects, defined or not
mcqs.why: A set is a well-defined collection of objects, and each object in it is called a member or element. 'Well-defined' means we can always decide whether a given object belongs to the set or not.

mcqs.q: What does the symbol ∈ mean?
mcqs.why: The symbol ∈ means 'is a member of', so x ∈ A says that x is an element of the set A. In the notes, N, Z, Q, R, P and O are used for natural numbers, integers, rationals, reals, primes and odd numbers.

mcqs.q: The set {x | x ∈ N and x < 4} in tabular form is:
mcqs.why: In tabular form all members are listed inside curly brackets. The natural numbers less than 4 are 1, 2 and 3, so the set is {1, 2, 3}; 4 is not included because the condition is x < 4, not x ≤ 4.

mcqs.q: A set which has no member at all is called:
mcqs.why: A set with no member is called an empty set and is denoted by ∅. It is different from a singleton set, which has exactly one member, and from infinite sets, whose members never come to an end.

mcqs.q: The set E = {z | z ∈ R and z² = 121} in tabular form is:
mcqs.why: We need every real z with z² = 121. Since 11² = 121 and (-11)² = 121 as well, both 11 and -11 satisfy the condition, so E = {-11, 11}. Taking only 11 would miss the negative root.

mcqs.q: Two sets are called equal sets when:
options: They have the same number of members
They have exactly the same members
One is a subset of the other
mcqs.why: Equal sets have exactly the same members. Sets with only the same number of members are called equivalent sets, which is a weaker condition, so equal sets must match member by member.

mcqs.q: The set of all prime numbers is an example of:
mcqs.why: A finite set has members that can be counted and come to an end. The prime numbers never come to an end, so the set of all prime numbers is an infinite set, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: If every member of A is also in B, then A is called:
mcqs.why: When every member of A is also a member of B, A is a subset of B, written A ⊆ B. If also A ≠ B it becomes a proper subset, and every set is an improper subset of itself.

mcqs.q: A set has n members. The number of subsets in its power set is:
mcqs.why: The power set is the set of all subsets of a set, and if the set has n members the number of subsets is 2^n. For example, a 3-member set has 2³ = 8 subsets, counting the empty set and the set itself.

mcqs.q: The power set of A = {5, 10, 15} has how many members?
mcqs.why: A has 3 members, so the number of subsets is 2³ = 8: ∅, {5}, {10}, {15}, {5, 10}, {5, 15}, {10, 15} and {5, 10, 15}. Hence the power set P(A) has exactly 8 members.

lessons.title: Exercise 17.2 — Operations on Sets: Union, Intersection, Difference and Complement
lessons.notes_html:
Disjoint, Overlapping, Exhaustive Sets and Partitions

If two sets have no common member, they are disjoint sets. If some members are common and neither set is a subset of the other, they are overlapping sets. If the union of two sets equals the whole universal set U, they are exhaustive sets. Disjoint and exhaustive sets together form a partition of U.

A ∩ B = ∅ ⇒ disjoint sets

A ∪ B = U ⇒ exhaustive sets

Union and Intersection

Putting together all the members of two sets is called their union. The members common to both form their intersection.

A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B}

A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B}

Difference and Symmetric Difference

A - B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B}

AΔB = (A ∪ B) - (A ∩ B) = (A - B) ∪ (B - A)

The symmetric difference contains the members which are in only one of the sets, not common to both.

Complement of a Set

A' = U - A

A' contains all those members of U which are not in A.

Worked Example: All Operations

Example: For A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and B = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}, find A ∪ B, A ∩ B, A - B, B - A and AΔB.

Step 1: Collect all members of both without repetition: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10}.

Step 2: Pick the common members: A ∩ B = {2, 4, 6}.

Step 3: Members of A which are not in B: A - B = {1, 3, 5}.

Step 4: Members of B which are not in A: B - A = {8, 10}.

Step 5: AΔB = (A ∪ B) - (A ∩ B) = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10} - {2, 4, 6}.

Step 6: So AΔB = {1, 3, 5, 8, 10}.

Worked Example: Complement

Example: For U = {1, 2, 3, ..., 10}, A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, B = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}, compare (A ∪ B)' and A' ∩ B'.

Step 1: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9}.

Step 2: (A ∪ B)' = U - {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9} = {6, 8, 10}.

Step 3: A' = {6, 7, 8, 9, 10} and B' = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}.

Step 4: A' ∩ B' = {6, 8, 10}.

Step 5: Both answers are the same, so (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' is verified.

mcqs.q: Two sets with no common member are called:
mcqs.why: If two sets have no common member, they are disjoint sets, and this is written A ∩ B = ∅. Overlapping sets share some members, while exhaustive sets have union equal to the whole universal set U.

mcqs.q: If A ∪ B = U, the sets A and B are called:
mcqs.why: When the union of two sets equals the whole universal set U, they are exhaustive sets. Disjoint and exhaustive sets together form a partition of U, as explained in the notes.

mcqs.q: The union A ∪ B is the set of members that are:
options: In A but not in B
In A or in B (or both)
mcqs.why: The union puts together all the members of the two sets: A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B}. Members common to both are the intersection, not the union, so 'or' is the key word for union.

The intersection contains only the members common to both sets. Comparing A and B, the common members are 2, 4 and 6, so A ∩ B = {2, 4, 6}. The full list without repetition is the union, not the intersection.

mcqs.q: For the same A and B, A − B is:
mcqs.why: A − B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B}, so we keep the members of A that are not in B. From A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, removing 2, 4 and 6 leaves A − B = {1, 3, 5}.

mcqs.q: The symmetric difference AΔB contains the members that are:
options: In only one of the sets
mcqs.why: AΔB = (A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B) = (A − B) ∪ (B − A), so it contains exactly the members which are in only one of the sets, not common to both. For the example sets, AΔB = {1, 3, 5, 8, 10}.

mcqs.q: The complement of a set A is:
mcqs.why: The complement A' contains all those members of the universal set U which are not in A, so A' = U − A. For U = {1, ..., 10} and A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, this gives A' = {6, 7, 8, 9, 10}.
First A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9}. Removing these from U = {1, ..., 10} leaves (A ∪ B)' = {6, 8, 10}, which also equals A' ∩ B', verifying De Morgan's law for this example.

mcqs.q: Which pair of sets forms a partition of U?
mcqs.why: The notes state that disjoint and exhaustive sets together form a partition of U: disjoint means no common member, and exhaustive means their union is the whole of U, so together they split U completely without overlap.
B − A keeps the members of B that are not in A. B = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}, and 2, 4, 6 are in A, leaving B − A = {8, 10}. Note that difference is not commutative: A − B = {1, 3, 5} is a different set.

lessons.title: Exercise 17.3 — Properties of Set Operations and De Morgan's Laws
lessons.notes_html:
Commutative Property

In union and intersection, changing the order does not change the answer.

A ∪ B = B ∪ A

A ∩ B = B ∩ A

Associative Property

For three sets, changing the grouping does not change the answer.

A ∪ (B ∪ C) = (A ∪ B) ∪ C

A ∩ (B ∩ C) = (A ∩ B) ∩ C

Distributive Property

A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C)

A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C)

De Morgan's Laws

(A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'

(A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'

Remember: on taking the complement, ∪ changes to ∩ and ∩ changes to ∪.

Absorption and Other Results

A ∪ (A ∩ B) = A and A ∩ (A ∪ B) = A

A ∪ B = A ∪ (A' ∩ B)

B = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A' ∩ B)

Worked Example: Verifying the Laws

Example: For U = {1, 2, ..., 12}, A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}, B = {2, 4, 6, 8}, check De Morgan's first law.

Step 1: First find A ∪ B: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12}.

Step 2: Take its complement: (A ∪ B)' = U - {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12} = {5, 7, 9, 10, 11}.

Step 3: Now find the separate complements: A' = U - A = {5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11} and B' = U - B = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12}.

Step 4: Take their intersection: A' ∩ B' = {5, 7, 9, 10, 11}, because 8 is not in B'.

Step 5: Both sides are {5, 7, 9, 10, 11}.

Step 6: Both sides are equal, so (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' is verified.

Worked Example: Proof

Example: Prove that A ∪ B = A ∪ (A' ∩ B).

Step 1: Apply the distributive property on the right side: A ∪ (A' ∩ B) = (A ∪ A') ∩ (A ∪ B).

Step 2: A ∪ A' = U.

Step 3: So the right side = U ∩ (A ∪ B) = A ∪ B.

Step 4: This equals the left side, so the proof is complete.

mcqs.q: The commutative property for union states that:
mcqs.why: In union and intersection, changing the order does not change the answer: A ∪ B = B ∪ A and A ∩ B = B ∩ A. Changing the grouping instead is the associative property, which is a different law.

mcqs.q: Which equality shows the associative property?
mcqs.why: For three sets, changing the grouping does not change the answer: A ∩ (B ∩ C) = (A ∩ B) ∩ C, and similarly for union. The second option is commutativity and the third is De Morgan's law, not associativity.

mcqs.q: The distributive property gives A ∪ (B ∩ C) equal to:
mcqs.why: Union distributes over intersection: A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C). The other distributive form is A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C), where intersection distributes over union.

mcqs.q: De Morgan's first law states that (A ∪ B)' equals:
mcqs.why: De Morgan's laws say (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'. The key point from the notes is that on taking the complement, ∪ changes to ∩ and ∩ changes to ∪.

mcqs.q: According to De Morgan's second law, (A ∩ B)' equals:
mcqs.why: By De Morgan's second law, (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B': the complement of the intersection is the union of the complements. Remember that taking the complement swaps union and intersection in the result.

mcqs.q: The absorption law states that A ∪ (A ∩ B) equals:
mcqs.why: The absorption results are A ∪ (A ∩ B) = A and A ∩ (A ∪ B) = A. Since A ∩ B is already inside A, uniting it with A adds nothing new, so the union stays equal to A itself.

mcqs.q: Which of these results is correct?
mcqs.why: The notes list A ∪ B = A ∪ (A' ∩ B) as a correct result. Its proof uses distribution: A ∪ (A' ∩ B) = (A ∪ A') ∩ (A ∪ B) = U ∩ (A ∪ B) = A ∪ B, since A ∪ A' = U.
A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12}, so its complement in U = {1, ..., 12} is {5, 7, 9, 10, 11}. This matches A' ∩ B' in the worked example, verifying De Morgan's first law numerically.

mcqs.q: In the proof that A ∪ (A' ∩ B) = A ∪ B, the step A ∪ A' is replaced by:
mcqs.why: A set united with its own complement gives the whole universal set, so A ∪ A' = U. Then U ∩ (A ∪ B) = A ∪ B, because intersecting with U changes nothing, which completes the proof.

mcqs.q: In the De Morgan verification with U = {1, ..., 12}, why is 8 not in A' ∩ B'?
mcqs.why: A' = {5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11} contains 8, but B' = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12} does not, because 8 ∈ B. An intersection needs the member in both sets, so 8 is excluded from A' ∩ B'.

lessons.title: Exercise 17.4 — Verification of Operations by Venn Diagrams
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Venn Diagram?

In a Venn diagram the universal set U is shown by a rectangle and the other sets by circles. The part which is shaded shows the required operation.

Diagram of Disjoint Sets

For disjoint sets, two separate circles are drawn which have no common part. In this case:

A ∩ B = ∅, AΔB = A ∪ B, A - B = A

Diagram of Overlapping Sets

For overlapping sets, two intersecting circles are drawn. The middle common part is A ∩ B and A - B is only the crescent-shaped part of A.

AΔB = (A ∪ B) - (A ∩ B)

Diagram of a Subset

If A ⊆ B, the small circle of A is drawn inside the big circle of B. In this case:

A ∩ B = A, A ∪ B = B, A - B = ∅

Worked Example: Verification of De Morgan's Law

Example: For U = {1, ..., 10}, A = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}, B = {5, 6, 7, 8}, check (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'.

Step 1: A ∪ B = {1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9}.

Step 2: (A ∪ B)' = U - {1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9} = {2, 4, 10}.

Step 3: A' = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} and B' = {1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10}.

Step 4: A' ∩ B' = {2, 4, 10}.

Step 5: Both sides are {2, 4, 10}, so the law is verified. In the diagram, the part outside both circles is shaded.

Worked Example: Verification of the Distributive Property

Example: For A = {1, ..., 8}, B = {4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10}, C = {5, 7, 9, 11}, check A ∩ (B ∪ C).

Step 1: B ∪ C = {4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11}.

Step 2: A ∩ (B ∪ C) = {4, 5, 6, 7, 8}.

Step 3: A ∩ B = {4, 6, 7, 8} and A ∩ C = {5, 7}.

Step 4: (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) = {4, 5, 6, 7, 8}.

Step 5: Both sides are equal, so the distributive property is verified.

mcqs.q: In a Venn diagram, the universal set U is shown by:
mcqs.why: In a Venn diagram the universal set U is shown by a rectangle and the other sets by circles drawn inside it. The part which is shaded shows the required operation being verified.

mcqs.q: For disjoint sets, the Venn diagram shows:
options: Two separate circles with no common part
mcqs.why: Disjoint sets have no common member, so two separate circles are drawn which have no common part. In this case A ∩ B = ∅, A − B = A and AΔB = A ∪ B, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: If A ⊆ B in a Venn diagram, then A − B equals:
mcqs.why: When A is a subset of B, the small circle of A lies inside the big circle of B, so nothing of A lies outside B. Hence A − B = ∅, while A ∩ B = A and A ∪ B = B.

mcqs.q: In the diagram of overlapping sets, the middle common part represents:
mcqs.why: For overlapping sets, two intersecting circles are drawn and the middle common part is A ∩ B. The set A − B is only the crescent-shaped part of A that lies outside B.
A ∪ B = {1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9}, so removing it from U leaves {2, 4, 10}. Also A' ∩ B' = {2, 4, 10}, so both sides agree; in the diagram this is the part outside both circles.

mcqs.q: In the same verification, the set A' is:
mcqs.why: A' = U − A, so from U = {1, ..., 10} we remove A = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}, giving A' = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}. Similarly B' = {1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10}, and their intersection is {2, 4, 10}.
First B ∪ C = {4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11}. Intersecting with A = {1, ..., 8} keeps {4, 5, 6, 7, 8}. This equals (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C), verifying the distributive property.

mcqs.q: In that distributive check, (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) is:
mcqs.why: A ∩ B = {4, 6, 7, 8} and A ∩ C = {5, 7}. Their union is {4, 5, 6, 7, 8}, exactly the same as A ∩ (B ∪ C), so the distributive property A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) is verified.

mcqs.q: For two disjoint sets, the symmetric difference AΔB equals:
mcqs.why: For disjoint sets, A ∩ B = ∅, so AΔB = (A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B) = (A ∪ B) − ∅ = A ∪ B. Nothing is removed from the union because the sets share no member at all.

mcqs.q: When A ⊆ B, the union A ∪ B equals:
mcqs.why: If every member of A is already in B, then uniting them adds nothing beyond B, so A ∪ B = B. In the same situation A ∩ B = A, because the whole of A is common to both sets.

lessons.title: Exercise 17.5 — Ordered Pairs, Cartesian Product, Relations and Functions
lessons.notes_html:
Ordered Pair and Cartesian Product

(a, b) is called an ordered pair. Two ordered pairs are equal when their first members are equal to each other and their second members are equal to each other.

(a, b) = (c, d) ⇒ a = c and b = d

A × B = {(a, b) | a ∈ A and b ∈ B}

O(A × B) = O(A) × O(B)

Binary Relation

Any subset of A × B is called a binary relation from A to B. If O(A) = m and O(B) = n, then the total number of relations is as follows.

Number of relations = 2^(m × n)

Domain and Range

The set of the first members of the pairs of a relation is called its domain, and the set of the second members is called its range.

Function and Its Types

A relation is a function if every member of the domain has only one image. A function is into if some member of the codomain has no pre-image; it is onto (surjective) if every member of the codomain has a pre-image; and if it is both one-one and onto, it is bijective, that is, a one-one correspondence.

Worked Example: Ordered Pairs

Example: From (2x - 3y, 5x + y) = (3, 16), find x and y.

Step 1: Equate the first members: 2x - 3y = 3.

Step 2: Equate the second members: 5x + y = 16, so y = 16 - 5x.

Step 3: Put the value of y in the first equation: 2x - 3(16 - 5x) = 3.

Step 4: Expand: 2x - 48 + 15x = 3, that is, 17x = 51.

Step 5: So x = 3 and y = 16 - 5(3) = 1.

Step 6: Check: 2(3) - 3(1) = 3 and 5(3) + 1 = 16; both are correct.

Worked Example: Domain and Range

Example: For R = {(x, y) | y = 2x + 5} and domain {-2, -1, 0, 1, 2}, find the range.

Step 1: Putting x = -2 gives y = 2(-2) + 5 = 1.

Step 2: Putting x = -1 gives y = 3.

Step 3: Putting x = 0 gives y = 5.

Step 4: Putting x = 1 gives y = 7.

Step 5: Putting x = 2 gives y = 9.

Step 6: So the range = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}.

mcqs.q: Two ordered pairs (a, b) and (c, d) are equal when:
mcqs.why: Two ordered pairs are equal when their first members are equal to each other and their second members are equal to each other: (a, b) = (c, d) implies a = c and b = d. Order matters, unlike in ordinary sets.

mcqs.q: The Cartesian product A × B is the set of:
options: All members of A and B together
All ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B
mcqs.why: A × B = {(a, b) | a ∈ A and b ∈ B}: every first member comes from A and every second member from B. Its order satisfies O(A × B) = O(A) × O(B).

mcqs.q: If O(A) = m and O(B) = n, the total number of binary relations from A to B is:
mcqs.why: Any subset of A × B is a binary relation from A to B. Since A × B has mn members, the number of its subsets, and so the number of relations, is 2^(mn), as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: The domain of a relation is the set of:
options: All first members of its pairs
All second members of its pairs
mcqs.why: The set of the first members of the pairs of a relation is called its domain, and the set of the second members is called its range. For example, in y = 2x + 5 the domain values are the x-values used.

mcqs.q: A relation is a function when:
options: Every codomain member has a pre-image
Every member of the domain has only one image
mcqs.why: A relation is a function if every member of the domain has only one image. If in addition every codomain member has a pre-image it is onto, and a function that is both one-one and onto is bijective.

mcqs.q: From (2x − 3y, 5x + y) = (3, 16), the values of x and y are:
mcqs.why: Equating members: 2x − 3y = 3 and 5x + y = 16, so y = 16 − 5x. Substituting gives 2x − 3(16 − 5x) = 3, that is 17x = 51, so x = 3 and y = 16 − 15 = 1, which checks in both equations.

mcqs.q: For R = {(x, y) | y = 2x + 5} with domain {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2}, the range is:
mcqs.why: Putting x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 into y = 2x + 5 gives y = 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 respectively. So the range, the set of second members actually obtained, is {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}.

mcqs.q: A function is called onto (surjective) when:
options: Some codomain member has no pre-image
Every member of the domain has one image
Every member of the codomain has a pre-image
mcqs.why: A function is onto (surjective) if every member of the codomain has a pre-image. If some codomain member has no pre-image, the function is only into, as the notes distinguish.

mcqs.q: A bijective function is one that is:
mcqs.why: A function that is both one-one and onto is bijective, that is, a one-one correspondence. Every domain member then pairs with exactly one codomain member and every codomain member is used.

mcqs.q: If O(A) = 3 and O(B) = 4, then O(A × B) is:
mcqs.why: The number of ordered pairs in A × B is the product of the numbers of members: O(A × B) = O(A) × O(B) = 3 × 4 = 12, since each of the 3 first members can pair with each of the 4 second members.

lessons.title: Exercise 18.1 — Ratio and Proportion
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Ratio?

The comparison of two quantities of the same kind is called a ratio. A ratio is written as a:b or a/b. Before writing a ratio, both quantities must be brought into the same unit. The first term of a ratio is called the antecedent and the second term the consequent.

What is a Proportion?

The equality of two ratios is called a proportion. If a:b :: c:d, then the product of the extreme terms equals the product of the mean terms.

a/b = c/d ⇒ a × d = b × c

Worked Example: Ratio in Simplest Form

Example: Find the ratio of 60 cm and 1 metre.

Step 1: Bring both into the same unit: 1 metre = 100 cm.

Step 2: Write the ratio: 60 : 100.

Step 3: Divide both by 20: 60 ÷ 20 = 3 and 100 ÷ 20 = 5.

Step 4: So the ratio = 3 : 5.

Worked Example: Finding x from a Proportion

Example: Find x from 2x + 5 : 5 :: 3x - 2 : 7.

Step 1: Write the proportion in fraction form: (2x + 5)/5 = (3x - 2)/7.

Step 2: Cross-multiply: 7(2x + 5) = 5(3x - 2).

Step 3: Expand: 14x + 35 = 15x - 10.

Step 4: Bring the x terms to one side: 35 + 10 = 15x - 14x.

Step 5: So x = 45.

Worked Example: Using a Given Ratio

Example: If a : b = 5 : 8, find 3a + 4b : 5a + 7b.

Step 1: Put a = 5k and b = 8k.

Step 2: 3a + 4b = 3(5k) + 4(8k) = 15k + 32k = 47k.

Step 3: 5a + 7b = 5(5k) + 7(8k) = 25k + 56k = 81k.

Step 4: The ratio = 47k : 81k = 47 : 81.

mcqs.q: A ratio is the comparison of two quantities that are:
mcqs.why: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind, written as a:b or a/b. Before writing a ratio both quantities must be brought into the same unit, as in the centimetre and metre example of the notes.

mcqs.q: In the ratio a : b, the first term a is called the:
mcqs.why: The first term of a ratio is called the antecedent and the second term is called the consequent. In a proportion a:b :: c:d, the outer terms a and d are the extremes and the inner terms are the means.

mcqs.q: The ratio of 60 cm to 1 metre in simplest form is:
mcqs.why: First bring both to the same unit: 1 metre = 100 cm, so the ratio is 60 : 100. Dividing both terms by 20 gives 3 : 5, which is the simplest form, exactly as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: If a/b = c/d, then which equality always holds?
mcqs.why: In a proportion, the product of the extreme terms equals the product of the mean terms: a/b = c/d implies a × d = b × c. This cross-multiplication is the basic tool for solving proportion questions.

mcqs.q: From 2x + 5 : 5 :: 3x − 2 : 7, the value of x is:
mcqs.why: Write (2x + 5)/5 = (3x − 2)/7 and cross-multiply: 7(2x + 5) = 5(3x − 2), so 14x + 35 = 15x − 10. Bringing the x terms together gives 35 + 10 = 15x − 14x, hence x = 45.

mcqs.q: If a : b = 5 : 8, then 3a + 4b : 5a + 7b equals:
mcqs.why: Put a = 5k and b = 8k. Then 3a + 4b = 15k + 32k = 47k and 5a + 7b = 25k + 56k = 81k. The ratio is 47k : 81k = 47 : 81, since the common factor k cancels.

mcqs.q: Before writing a ratio of two lengths in different units, we must:
options: Bring both into the same unit
mcqs.why: A ratio compares quantities of the same kind, so both must be in the same unit first. In the notes, 1 metre is changed to 100 cm before the ratio 60 : 100 is written and simplified.

mcqs.q: The equality of two ratios is called a:
mcqs.why: The equality of two ratios is called a proportion, written a:b :: c:d. A single comparison a:b is only a ratio; two equal ratios together make a proportion.

mcqs.q: If 3 : 5 :: x : 20, then x equals:
mcqs.why: By the extremes and means rule, 3 × 20 = 5 × x, so 60 = 5x and x = 12. Checking: 3/5 = 0.6 and 12/20 = 0.6, so the two ratios are indeed equal.

mcqs.q: In a proportion, the product of the means equals:
mcqs.why: For a:b :: c:d, the product of the extreme terms equals the product of the mean terms: a × d = b × c. So the product of the means b × c is exactly the product of the extremes a × d.

lessons.title: Exercise 18.2 — Direct and Inverse Variation
lessons.notes_html:
Direct Variation

If, on increasing one quantity, the other also increases in the same ratio, it is called direct variation.

y ∝ x ⇒ y = kx

k is called the constant of variation. If y varies directly as x², we write y = kx².

Inverse Variation

If, on increasing one quantity, the other decreases, it is called inverse variation.

y ∝ 1/x ⇒ y = k/x

Similarly, if y ∝ 1/r², we write y = k/r².

Method

Step 1: Change the variation into an equation by including k. Step 2: Put the given values and find k. Step 3: Put the new value and find the required quantity.

Worked Example: Direct Variation

Example: y varies directly as x and y = 10 when x = 3. Find y when x = 6.

Step 1: Write y = kx.

Step 2: Put the given values: 10 = 3k, so k = 10/3.

Step 3: The equation becomes: y = (10/3)x.

Step 4: Put x = 6: y = (10/3) × 6 = 20.

Step 5: So y = 20.

Worked Example: Inverse Variation

Example: y varies inversely as x and y = 10 when x = 3. Find y when x = 10.

Step 1: Write y = k/x.

Step 2: From 10 = k/3 we get k = 30.

Step 3: The equation becomes: y = 30/x.

Step 4: Put x = 10: y = 30/10 = 3.

Step 5: So y = 3.

mcqs.q: If y varies directly as x, the equation of variation is:
mcqs.why: In direct variation one quantity increases in the same ratio as the other, written y ∝ x, which becomes the equation y = kx. Here k is called the constant of variation, found from a given pair of values.

mcqs.q: y varies directly as x, and y = 10 when x = 3. When x = 6, y equals:
mcqs.why: From y = kx, 10 = 3k gives k = 10/3, so y = (10/3)x. Putting x = 6 gives y = (10/3) × 6 = 20. Doubling x from 3 to 6 doubles y, as direct variation requires.

mcqs.q: If y varies inversely as x, then y equals:
mcqs.why: In inverse variation, increasing one quantity decreases the other, written y ∝ 1/x, which becomes y = k/x. The constant k is found first from the given values, and then the required value is computed.

mcqs.q: y varies inversely as x, and y = 10 when x = 3. When x = 10, y equals:
mcqs.why: From y = k/x, 10 = k/3 gives k = 30, so y = 30/x. Putting x = 10 gives y = 30/10 = 3. Note how the answer fell from 10 to 3 when x grew, which is the mark of inverse variation.

mcqs.q: The constant k in a variation equation is called:
mcqs.why: k is called the constant of variation. The method of the lesson is: change the variation into an equation with k, put the given values to find k, then put the new value to find the required quantity.

mcqs.q: If y varies directly as x², the correct equation is:
mcqs.why: The notes state that if y varies directly as x², we write y = kx². Similarly, if y varies inversely as r², we write y = k/r²; the power stays with the variable, and only the position (numerator or denominator) changes.

mcqs.q: In inverse variation, when one quantity is doubled, the other:
mcqs.why: Since y = k/x, the product xy = k stays constant. Doubling x therefore halves y, because x × y must remain equal to the same constant k. This is the opposite behaviour of direct variation.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct first step in solving a variation question?
options: Put the new value at once
Change the variation into an equation by including k
Take square roots of both sides
mcqs.why: The method is in three steps: first change the variation into an equation by including k, then put the given values and find k, and finally put the new value and find the required quantity.

mcqs.q: If y = kx and y = 24 when x = 8, then k equals:
mcqs.why: Putting the given values into y = kx: 24 = 8k, so k = 24/8 = 3. Once k is known, the equation y = 3x can be used for any other value of x, which is the standard method of this lesson.

mcqs.q: If y ∝ 1/r² and r is doubled, then y becomes:
mcqs.why: With y = k/r², doubling r makes the denominator (2r)² = 4r², four times as big. So y becomes one quarter of its former value, because the denominator grew by the square of the factor 2.

lessons.title: Exercise 18.3 — Third, Fourth and Mean Proportionals
lessons.notes_html:
Fourth Proportional

If a : b :: c : x, then x is called the fourth proportional to a, b, c.

x = (b × c)/a

Third Proportional

If a : b :: x : d, then x is called the third proportional, and it is found by the following formula.

x = (a × d)/b

Mean Proportional and Continued Proportion

If a, m, b are in continued proportion, that is, a : m :: m : b, then m is called the mean proportional of a and b.

m² = a × b ⇒ m = √(a × b)

Worked Example: Mean Proportional

Example: Find the mean proportional of 8 and 18.

Step 1: Suppose the mean proportional is m; then 8 : m :: m : 18.

Step 2: Equate the products of the extremes and the means: m² = 8 × 18.

Step 3: m² = 144.

Step 4: Take the square root of both sides: m = 12.

Step 5: So the mean proportional is 12.

Worked Example: Fourth Proportional

Example: Find the fourth proportional to 8, 4, 2.

Step 1: Write the proportion: 8 : 4 :: 2 : x.

Step 2: Cross-multiply: 8x = 4 × 2 = 8.

Step 3: x = 8/8 = 1.

Step 4: So the fourth proportional is 1.

Worked Example: Continued Proportion

Example: 45, x, 5 are in continued proportion; find x.

Step 1: In continued proportion the square of the middle term equals the product of the two extremes: x² = 45 × 5.

Step 2: x² = 225.

Step 3: x = 15.

mcqs.q: If a : b :: c : x, then x is called the:
options: Fourth proportional to a, b, c
mcqs.why: If a : b :: c : x, then x is called the fourth proportional to a, b, c, and it is found by x = (b × c)/a, using the rule that the product of extremes equals the product of means.

mcqs.q: The fourth proportional to 8, 4, 2 is:
mcqs.why: Write 8 : 4 :: 2 : x. Cross-multiplying, 8x = 4 × 2 = 8, so x = 8/8 = 1. Hence the fourth proportional to 8, 4 and 2 is 1, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: If a, m, b are in continued proportion, then m is:
options: The sum of a and b
The mean proportional of a and b
mcqs.why: If a : m :: m : b, then m is called the mean proportional of a and b. It satisfies m² = a × b, so m = √(a × b); it is the middle term that appears in both ratios of the continued proportion.

mcqs.q: The mean proportional of 8 and 18 is:
mcqs.why: Let the mean proportional be m; then m² = 8 × 18 = 144. Taking the square root, m = 12. Check: 8 : 12 :: 12 : 18, since both ratios equal 2 : 3, confirming 12 is correct.

mcqs.q: If 45, x, 5 are in continued proportion, then x equals:
mcqs.why: In continued proportion the square of the middle term equals the product of the extremes: x² = 45 × 5 = 225. Taking the square root gives x = 15, exactly as worked out in the notes.

mcqs.q: The formula for the fourth proportional x in a : b :: c : x is:
mcqs.why: From a/b = c/x, cross-multiplication gives a × x = b × c, so x = (b × c)/a. This is the product of the two mean terms divided by the first extreme, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: The mean proportional of 4 and 25 is:
mcqs.why: The mean proportional m satisfies m = √(a × b) = √(4 × 25) = √100 = 10. Indeed 4 : 10 :: 10 : 25 because both ratios reduce to 2 : 5, so 10 is the mean proportional.

mcqs.q: If a : b :: x : d, then x, as given in the notes, is called the:
mcqs.why: The notes define: if a : b :: x : d, then x is called the third proportional, found by x = (a × d)/b. It differs from the fourth proportional, where the unknown is the last term of the proportion.

mcqs.q: In continued proportion a : m :: m : b, which relation holds?
mcqs.why: Applying extremes and means to a : m :: m : b gives a × b = m × m, that is, m² = a × b. This is why the mean proportional is the square root of the product of the two given numbers.

mcqs.q: The third proportional formula given in the notes, for a : b :: x : d, is:
mcqs.why: From a/b = x/d, cross-multiplying gives b × x = a × d, so x = (a × d)/b. This is the formula the notes give for the third proportional, with the product of the extremes divided by the second term.

lessons.title: Exercise 18.4 — Proofs and Solutions by Componendo and Dividendo
lessons.notes_html:
What are Componendo and Dividendo?

If a/b = c/d, then taking the sum and difference of the numerator and denominator terms in each ratio is called componendo and dividendo.

(a + b)/(a - b) = (c + d)/(c - d)

By componendo alone we get (a + b)/b = (c + d)/d, and by dividendo alone (a - b)/b = (c - d)/d.

Easy Method of Proof: Putting k

In proofs, put x/y = z/w = k, that is, x = ky and z = kw. Then simplify both sides; both will give the same form in k and the proof is complete.

Worked Example: Proof

Example: If x : y = z : w, prove that (4x + 3y)/(4x - 3y) = (4z + 3w)/(4z - 3w).

Step 1: Put x/y = z/w = k, so x = ky and z = kw.

Step 2: Left side = (4ky + 3y)/(4ky - 3y).

Step 3: Take y common from the top and bottom: = (4k + 3)/(4k - 3).

Step 4: Right side = (4kw + 3w)/(4kw - 3w).

Step 5: Taking w common, the right side also becomes (4k + 3)/(4k - 3).

Step 6: Both sides are equal, so the proof is complete.

Worked Example: Solving an Equation

Example: Solve (√(x + 5) - √(x - 5))/(√(x + 5) + √(x - 5)) = 1/10.

Step 1: Invert: (√(x + 5) + √(x - 5))/(√(x + 5) - √(x - 5)) = 10/1.

Step 2: Apply componendo-dividendo: (2√(x + 5))/(2√(x - 5)) = 11/9.

Step 3: Square both sides: (x + 5)/(x - 5) = 121/81.

Step 4: Cross-multiply: 81x + 405 = 121x - 605.

Step 5: 405 + 605 = 121x - 81x, that is, 40x = 1010.

Step 6: So x = 101/4.

mcqs.q: If a/b = c/d, applying componendo and dividendo gives:
mcqs.why: Componendo and dividendo means taking the sum and difference of the numerator and denominator terms in each ratio: from a/b = c/d we get (a + b)/(a − b) = (c + d)/(c − d), as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: By componendo alone, from a/b = c/d we get:
mcqs.why: By componendo alone we get (a + b)/b = (c + d)/d: only the sum is taken, over the denominator. By dividendo alone we instead get (a − b)/b = (c − d)/d, using the difference.

mcqs.q: In the easy method of proof for equal ratios, we put:
options: x/y = z/w = k, so x = ky and z = kw
mcqs.why: In proofs, put x/y = z/w = k, that is, x = ky and z = kw. Then simplifying both sides gives the same form in k, and the proof is complete. This k-method is the easy method of the lesson.

mcqs.q: If x : y = z : w, then (4x + 3y)/(4x − 3y) equals:
mcqs.why: Put x/y = z/w = k, so x = ky and z = kw. The left side becomes (4k + 3)/(4k − 3) after taking y common, and the right side (4z + 3w)/(4z − 3w) becomes the same after taking w common, proving the equality.
Invert to 10/1, then componendo-dividendo gives √(x + 5)/√(x − 5) = 11/9. Squaring, (x + 5)/(x − 5) = 121/81, so 81x + 405 = 121x − 605, giving 40x = 1010 and x = 101/4.

mcqs.q: After inverting the equation in the worked example, componendo-dividendo gives the ratio:
mcqs.why: After inversion the ratio is 10/1. Componendo-dividendo turns it into (10 + 1)/(10 − 1) = 11/9, so (2√(x + 5))/(2√(x − 5)) = 11/9. Squaring this later produces 121/81, which is a subsequent step, not this one.

mcqs.q: Componendo and dividendo is applied to an equality of the form:
mcqs.why: Componendo and dividendo starts from an equality of two ratios, a/b = c/d. The sums and differences of numerator and denominator terms are then taken in each ratio to get the new equality.

mcqs.q: By dividendo alone, from a/b = c/d we get:
mcqs.why: By dividendo alone we get (a − b)/b = (c − d)/d: only the difference of numerator and denominator is taken, over the denominator. Componendo alone uses the sum instead, giving (a + b)/b = (c + d)/d.

mcqs.q: In the k-method proof, after putting x = ky, the expression (4x + 3y)/(4x − 3y) simplifies to:
mcqs.why: Substituting x = ky gives (4ky + 3y)/(4ky − 3y). Taking y common from numerator and denominator, the y cancels and leaves (4k + 3)/(4k − 3). The right side gives the identical form, completing the proof.

mcqs.q: The first step in solving the square-root equation of the worked example is to:
mcqs.why: The given fraction equals 1/10; the first step is to invert it, making it 10/1. Only then is componendo-dividendo applied, followed by squaring. Inverting first is what makes the sums and differences come out neatly.

lessons.title: Exercise 18.5 — Joint Variation
lessons.notes_html:
What is Joint Variation?

When one quantity changes in direct variation with two or more quantities and in inverse variation with others at the same time, it is called joint variation. Every direct quantity is written in the numerator and every inverse quantity in the denominator.

y ∝ x²z ⇒ y = kx²z

y ∝ x²u²/(tv) ⇒ y = kx²u²/(tv)

Method

Step 1: Write the joint variation as one equation containing the constant k. Step 2: Put the given values and find k. Step 3: Put the new values and find the answer.

Worked Example: Volume of a Gas

Example: The volume V of a gas varies directly as the temperature T and inversely as the pressure P. V = 100 when T = 30 and P = 64. Find V when T = 60 and P = 81.

Step 1: Write V = kT/P.

Step 2: Put the given values: 100 = k(30)/64.

Step 3: k = 100 × 64/30 = 640/3.

Step 4: Put the new values: V = (640/3) × 60/81.

Step 5: V = 12800/81 ≈ 158.02.

Worked Example: Time of a Pendulum

Example: The time T of a pendulum varies directly as the square root of the length L and inversely as the square root of g. T = 2 when L = 100 and g = 9.8. Find T when L = 200 and g = 7.6.

Step 1: Write T = k√L/√g = k√(L/g).

Step 2: From 2 = k√(100/9.8) we get k = √9.8/5.

Step 3: Put the new values: T = (√9.8/5)√(200/7.6).

Step 4: Simplify: T = 14/√19 ≈ 3.21 seconds.

mcqs.q: Joint variation means one quantity varies:
options: Directly with only one other quantity
Directly with some quantities and inversely with others at the same time
mcqs.why: When one quantity changes in direct variation with two or more quantities and in inverse variation with others at the same time, it is called joint variation. Direct quantities go in the numerator and inverse ones in the denominator.

mcqs.q: If y ∝ x²z, the equation is:
mcqs.why: Both x² and z are direct quantities, so both appear in the numerator: y ∝ x²z becomes y = kx²z. The constant k is then found from one set of given values before solving for new values.

mcqs.q: If y ∝ x²u²/(tv), the equation is:
mcqs.why: Every direct quantity is written in the numerator and every inverse quantity in the denominator: x² and u² are direct, t and v are inverse, so y = kx²u²/(tv), exactly as the notes write it.

mcqs.q: The volume V of a gas varies directly as T and inversely as P, with V = 100 when T = 30 and P = 64. The constant k is:
mcqs.why: Write V = kT/P and put the given values: 100 = k(30)/64. Solving, k = 100 × 64/30 = 640/3. This k is then used with the new values of T and P to find the new volume.

mcqs.q: For that gas, when T = 60 and P = 81, V is approximately:
mcqs.why: V = (640/3) × 60/81 = 12800/81 ≈ 158.02. The temperature doubled, which raised V, while the pressure rose from 64 to 81, which lowered it; the combined result is about 158.02.

mcqs.q: The time T of a pendulum varies directly as √L and inversely as √g, so T equals:
mcqs.why: Direct with √L and inverse with √g gives T = k√L/√g = k√(L/g), as the notes write. With the given values this leads to T = 14/√19 ≈ 3.21 seconds for the new length and gravity.

mcqs.q: In joint variation questions, k is found by:
options: Putting the given values into the equation
mcqs.why: The method is fixed: write the joint variation as one equation containing k, put the given values and find k, then put the new values and find the answer. Without k from the given data, the new values cannot be used.

mcqs.q: If S ∝ bd², then S equals:
mcqs.why: S varies directly as b and directly as the square of d, so both are numerator quantities: S = kbd². This is the beam-strength relation used in the practical questions lesson.

mcqs.q: A quantity varying directly as x and inversely as y² is written as:
mcqs.why: Direct quantities go in the numerator and inverse quantities in the denominator, with their powers kept: x is direct so it is on top, y² is inverse so it is underneath, giving z = kx/y² in the pattern of this lesson.

mcqs.q: In the pendulum example, T = 2 when L = 100 and g = 9.8 gave k equal to:
mcqs.why: From T = k√(L/g), 2 = k√(100/9.8) = k × 10/√9.8, so k = 2√9.8/10 = √9.8/5. Putting the new values L = 200, g = 7.6 with this k gives T ≈ 3.21 seconds.

lessons.title: Exercise 18.6 — More Proofs about Equal Ratios
lessons.notes_html:
Aim of This Lesson

In this exercise, harder results have to be proved from one or three equal ratios. The basic method of all the proofs is the same: put the equal ratio equal to k.

p/q = r/s = k ⇒ p = qk and r = sk

a/b = c/d = e/f = k ⇒ a = bk, c = dk, e = fk

Worked Example: Proof with One Ratio

Example: If p : q = r : s, prove that ∛((p³ + r³)/(q³ + s³)) = p/q.

Step 1: Put p/q = r/s = k, so p = qk and r = sk.

Step 2: p³ + r³ = q³k³ + s³k³ = k³(q³ + s³).

Step 3: Form the ratio: (p³ + r³)/(q³ + s³) = k³(q³ + s³)/(q³ + s³) = k³.

Step 4: Take the cube root of both sides: ∛(k³) = k.

Step 5: And k = p/q, so the required result is proved.

Worked Example: Proof with Powers

Example: Prove that p⁵ + r⁵ : q⁵ + s⁵ = p³r² : q³s².

Step 1: The left ratio = (p⁵ + r⁵)/(q⁵ + s⁵).

Step 2: Put p = qk and r = sk: = (q⁵k⁵ + s⁵k⁵)/(q⁵ + s⁵) = k⁵.

Step 3: The right ratio = p³r²/(q³s²) = (q³k³)(s²k²)/(q³s²) = k⁵.

Step 4: Both sides are k⁵, so the proof is complete.

Pattern for Three Ratios

In three equal ratios, on putting each first term = second term × k, a power of k comes out as a common factor from the upper part, as in (a²b + c²d + e²f)/(ab² + cd² + ef²), where the upper part becomes k²(b³ + d³ + f³) and the lower part k(b³ + d³ + f³), and the answer is k.

mcqs.q: The basic method of all the proofs in this lesson is to:
options: Put the equal ratio equal to k
mcqs.why: The basic method of all the proofs is the same: put the equal ratio equal to k. From p/q = r/s = k we write p = qk and r = sk, and then a power of k comes out as a common factor.

mcqs.q: If p/q = r/s = k, then p and r are written as:
options: p = q + k, r = s + k
mcqs.why: From p/q = k, multiplying by q gives p = qk; likewise r = sk. These two substitutions are the starting point of every proof in this exercise, for one ratio or for three equal ratios.

mcqs.q: If p : q = r : s, then ∛((p³ + r³)/(q³ + s³)) equals:
mcqs.why: Put p = qk and r = sk: p³ + r³ = k³(q³ + s³), so the fraction equals k³. Taking the cube root gives k, and k = p/q, so the result is p/q, as the worked example proves.

mcqs.q: The ratio (p⁵ + r⁵) : (q⁵ + s⁵) simplifies, with the k-method, to:
mcqs.why: Putting p = qk and r = sk, the numerator becomes q⁵k⁵ + s⁵k⁵ = k⁵(q⁵ + s⁵). Dividing by (q⁵ + s⁵) leaves k⁵. The notes use this to prove the ratio equals p³r² : q³s², which is also k⁵.

mcqs.q: For three equal ratios a/b = c/d = e/f = k, we write:
options: a = b/k, c = d/k, e = f/k
a = bk, c = dk, e = fk
a = b + k, c = d + k, e = f + k
a = kb, c = kd, e = kf with k = 0
mcqs.why: With three equal ratios, each first term equals its second term times k: a = bk, c = dk, e = fk. Then in expressions like (a²b + c²d + e²f)/(ab² + cd² + ef²), a power of k factors out top and bottom.

mcqs.q: In (a²b + c²d + e²f)/(ab² + cd² + ef²), the whole expression simplifies to:
mcqs.why: The upper part becomes k²(b³ + d³ + f³) and the lower part k(b³ + d³ + f³). Cancelling the common bracket leaves k²/k = k, which is the pattern the notes point out for three equal ratios.

mcqs.q: In the proof of ∛((p³ + r³)/(q³ + s³)) = p/q, the fraction before taking the cube root equals:
mcqs.why: Since p³ + r³ = q³k³ + s³k³ = k³(q³ + s³), dividing by (q³ + s³) leaves exactly k³. The cube root of k³ is k, and since k = p/q, the required result follows.

mcqs.q: The ratio p³r² : q³s² in the second worked example equals:
mcqs.why: p³r² = (q³k³)(s²k²) = q³s²k⁵, and dividing by q³s² leaves k⁵. The other side, (p⁵ + r⁵)/(q⁵ + s⁵), is also k⁵, so both sides agree and the proof is complete.

mcqs.q: Why does the k-method work for these proofs?
options: Because both sides reduce to the same power or form of k
Because q and s are equal
Because ratios can be inverted freely
mcqs.why: After substituting p = qk and r = sk, the common bracket cancels and each side reduces to the same power of k, such as k⁵ on both sides. Equal results in k means the two original sides are equal.

mcqs.q: If a/b = c/d = e/f = k, then e is written as:
mcqs.why: Each ratio equal to k means each numerator is the denominator times k: a = bk, c = dk and e = fk. This uniform substitution is what lets a power of k be factored out in the three-ratio proofs.

lessons.title: Exercise 18.7 — Practical Questions of Variation
lessons.notes_html:
Method for Practical Questions

The variation questions of daily life are also solved by the same three steps: write the variation as an equation with k, find k from the given values, then put the new values and find the answer. A quantity in direct variation is written in the numerator and a quantity in inverse variation in the denominator.

I = kV/R (electric current)

I = k/d² (intensity of light)

S = kbd² (strength of a beam)

C = knd (wages)

Worked Example: Strength of a Beam

Example: The strength S of a beam varies directly as its breadth b and directly as the square of its depth d. A beam 9 cm broad and 12 cm deep can bear 1200 pounds. How much weight will a beam 12 cm broad and 9 cm deep bear?

Step 1: Write S = kbd².

Step 2: Put the given values: 1200 = k × 9 × 144 = 1296k.

Step 3: k = 1200/1296 = 25/27.

Step 4: Put the new values: S = (25/27) × 12 × 81.

Step 5: S = (25/27) × 972 = 900.

Step 6: So the beam will bear 900 pounds.

Worked Example: Wages

Example: The amount C is in joint variation with the number of labourers n and the days d. The wages of 100 labourers for 20 days are 9000 rupees. Find the wages of 300 labourers for 15 days.

Step 1: Write C = knd.

Step 2: 9000 = k × 100 × 20 = 2000k, so k = 4.5.

Step 3: Put the new values: C = 4.5 × 300 × 15.

Step 4: C = 20250 rupees.

mcqs.q: The strength S of a beam varies as S = kbd². A beam 9 cm broad and 12 cm deep bears 1200 pounds; k equals:
mcqs.why: Put the values in S = kbd²: 1200 = k × 9 × 12² = 1296k. So k = 1200/1296 = 25/27. This constant is then used for the beam of different breadth and depth.

mcqs.q: That beam, when 12 cm broad and 9 cm deep, will bear:
mcqs.why: S = (25/27) × 12 × 9² = (25/27) × 12 × 81 = (25/27) × 972 = 900. So the new beam bears 900 pounds; the greater breadth did not compensate for the smaller depth, because depth is squared.

mcqs.q: Wages C vary jointly with labourers n and days d, C = knd. Wages of 100 labourers for 20 days are 9000 rupees, so k equals:
mcqs.why: 9000 = k × 100 × 20 = 2000k, so k = 9000/2000 = 4.5. The constant 4.5 is the wage per labourer per day under the given conditions, used for the next set of values.

mcqs.q: The wages of 300 labourers for 15 days are:
mcqs.why: C = knd = 4.5 × 300 × 15 = 4.5 × 4500 = 20250 rupees. The labourers tripled but the days fell from 20 to 15, so the wages a little more than doubled, from 9000 to 20250.

mcqs.q: The electric current relation in the notes is:
mcqs.why: The notes list I = kV/R for electric current: current varies directly as voltage V and inversely as resistance R. Direct quantities are written in the numerator and inverse ones in the denominator.

mcqs.q: The intensity of light is given by:
mcqs.why: The notes give I = k/d²: the intensity varies inversely as the square of the distance d. Doubling the distance would therefore make the intensity one quarter, because the denominator becomes four times as large.

mcqs.q: In every practical variation question, the quantity in inverse variation is written:
mcqs.why: The method says: a quantity in direct variation is written in the numerator and a quantity in inverse variation in the denominator. This single rule builds equations such as I = kV/R and V = kT/P correctly.

mcqs.q: The three steps for practical variation questions are:
options: Write the equation with k, find k, put new values
mcqs.why: The variation questions of daily life are solved by the same three steps: write the variation as an equation with k, find k from the given values, then put the new values and find the answer.

mcqs.q: For the wages relation C = knd, if n doubles and d stays the same, C:
mcqs.why: C = knd is directly proportional to n, so doubling the number of labourers with the same days doubles the wages. Only a squared quantity, like the depth in S = kbd², would give a four-times change.

mcqs.q: The strength of a beam varies directly as:
options: Breadth and the square of depth
mcqs.why: The notes state S varies directly as its breadth b and directly as the square of its depth d, giving S = kbd². The square on d is why reducing depth from 12 to 9 cut the strength so strongly in the example.

lessons.title: Exercise 19.1 — Types of Matrices, Addition, Subtraction and Multiplication
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Matrix?

A matrix is an arrangement of numbers written in rows and columns inside brackets [ ]. Each number of a matrix is called its element. The element aij means: the element of row number i and column number j.

Order of a Matrix

The order of a matrix is told by the number of its rows and columns.

Order = number of rows × number of columns

Example: Look at the matrix [3 4; -1 2; 0 3].

Step 1: Count the rows — there are 3 rows in it.

Step 2: Count the columns — there are 2 columns in it.

Step 3: So the order = 3 × 2.

Another example: The matrix [0] has only one row and one column, so its order is 1 × 1.

Types of Matrices

Row matrix: which has only one row, such as [-2 0].

Column matrix: which has only one column, such as [3; -1; 4].

Square matrix: in which the number of rows and columns is equal, such as [2 -1; 3 0], which is 2 × 2.

Rectangular matrix: in which the number of rows and columns is not equal, such as a 2 × 3 matrix.

Diagonal matrix: a square matrix in which all the elements except those on the main diagonal are zero, such as [a 0 0; 0 b 0; 0 0 c].

Scalar matrix: a diagonal matrix whose diagonal elements are all equal, such as [λ 0; 0 λ].

Symmetric matrix: whose transpose is equal to the matrix itself.

Aᵗ = A ⇒ symmetric matrix

Skew-symmetric matrix: whose transpose is equal to its negative. The diagonal elements of such a matrix are always zero.

Aᵗ = -A ⇒ skew-symmetric matrix

Example: [1 1 -1; 1 2 0; -1 0 5] is symmetric, because a12 = a21 = 1, a13 = a31 = -1 and a23 = a32 = 0. Whereas [0 1 -2; -1 0 3; 2 -3 0] is skew-symmetric, because every element is equal to the negative of the element on the other side of the diagonal, and the diagonal elements are zero.

Addition and Subtraction of Matrices

Two matrices can be added or subtracted only when they have the same order. In addition and subtraction, the corresponding elements are added or subtracted. For multiplication by a number, every element of the matrix is multiplied by that number.

Example: If A = [1 -1; 0 1] and C = [2 3; -1 2], find A + C.

Step 1: Add the elements of the first row: 1 + 2 = 3 and -1 + 3 = 2.

Step 2: Add the elements of the second row: 0 + (-1) = -1 and 1 + 2 = 3.

Step 3: So A + C = [3 2; -1 3].

Remember: If the order of A is 2 × 2 and the order of E is 3 × 3, then A + E is not possible, because the orders are different. In addition, changing the order does not change the answer:

A + B = B + A

Multiplication of Matrices

The product of two matrices is possible when the number of columns of the first matrix is equal to the number of rows of the second matrix.

A (m × n) × B (n × p) = AB (m × p)

In multiplication, a row of the first matrix is multiplied element by element with a column of the second matrix and the products are added. In general, changing the order in multiplication changes the answer:

In general AB ≠ BA

Example: For A = [1 -1; 0 1], find A².

Step 1: A² = A × A = [1 -1; 0 1] × [1 -1; 0 1].

Step 2: First row, first column: 1×1 + (-1)×0 = 1.

Step 3: First row, second column: 1×(-1) + (-1)×1 = -2.

Step 4: Second row, first column: 0×1 + 1×0 = 0.

Step 5: Second row, second column: 0×(-1) + 1×1 = 1.

Step 6: So A² = [1 -2; 0 1].

Other properties of multiplication: A(B + C) = AB + AC (distributive law) and A(BC) = (AB)C (associative law).

Equal Matrices and Unknown Elements

Two matrices are equal when they have the same order and their corresponding elements are equal. By this, unknown elements can be found.

Example: If [a b; c d] + [-3 1; 1 0] = [1 0; 0 1], find a, b, c, d.

Step 1: From the first element: a - 3 = 1, so a = 4.

Step 2: From the second element: b + 1 = 0, so b = -1.

Step 3: From the third element: c + 1 = 0, so c = -1.

Step 4: From the fourth element: d + 0 = 1, so d = 1.

mcqs.q: The element aij of a matrix means the element in:
mcqs.why: The element aij means the element of row number i and column number j: the first subscript is the row, the second is the column. This naming is used throughout the matrices lesson.

mcqs.q: The order of the matrix [3 4; −1 2; 0 3] is:
mcqs.why: Count the rows and columns: the matrix has 3 rows and 2 columns, so its order is 3 × 2 (rows × columns). The matrix [0] has one row and one column, so its order is 1 × 1.

mcqs.q: A matrix with only one row, such as [−2 0], is called a:
mcqs.why: A row matrix has only one row, like [−2 0]. A column matrix has only one column, and a square matrix has equal numbers of rows and columns; these names describe the shape of the matrix.

mcqs.q: A square matrix in which all elements except those on the main diagonal are zero is a:
mcqs.why: A diagonal matrix is a square matrix whose off-diagonal elements are all zero, such as [a 0 0; 0 b 0; 0 0 c]. If in addition all diagonal elements are equal, it is the special case called a scalar matrix.

mcqs.q: A matrix A is symmetric when:
mcqs.why: A symmetric matrix has its transpose equal to itself: Aᵗ = A, meaning aij = aji across the diagonal. If instead Aᵗ = −A, the matrix is skew-symmetric, and then its diagonal elements are always zero.

mcqs.q: Two matrices can be added only when:
mcqs.why: Two matrices can be added or subtracted only when they have the same order, and then corresponding elements are added or subtracted. A 2 × 2 and a 3 × 3 matrix cannot be added, as the notes warn.

mcqs.q: If A = [1 −1; 0 1] and C = [2 3; −1 2], then A + C is:
mcqs.why: Add corresponding elements: first row 1 + 2 = 3 and −1 + 3 = 2; second row 0 + (−1) = −1 and 1 + 2 = 3. So A + C = [3 2; −1 3], exactly as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: The product AB is possible when:
options: A and B have the same order
The number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B
The number of rows of A equals the number of columns of B
mcqs.why: A (m × n) × B (n × p) = AB (m × p): the inner numbers must match, so the columns of the first matrix must equal the rows of the second. The outer numbers m and p then give the order of the product.

mcqs.q: In general, for matrices, AB compared with BA is:
options: In general not equal: AB ≠ BA
mcqs.why: In general, changing the order in multiplication changes the answer: AB ≠ BA. This is a key difference from ordinary numbers, even though the associative and distributive laws do hold for matrices.

mcqs.q: If [a b; c d] + [−3 1; 1 0] = [1 0; 0 1], then a, b, c, d are:
mcqs.why: Compare corresponding elements: a − 3 = 1 gives a = 4; b + 1 = 0 gives b = −1; c + 1 = 0 gives c = −1; d + 0 = 1 gives d = 1. Equal matrices have the same order and equal corresponding elements.

lessons.title: Exercise 19.2 — Determinant, Adjoint, Multiplicative Inverse and Cramer's Rule
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Determinant?

With every square matrix a number is associated, which is called its determinant and is denoted by |A|. A determinant is only for a square matrix.

For a 2 × 2 matrix A = [a b; c d]:

|A| = ad - bc

Example: Find the value of |-5 -3; 3 -4|.

Step 1: Apply the formula: |A| = (-5)(-4) - (-3)(3).

Step 2: Multiply: 20 - (-9) = 20 + 9.

Step 3: So the determinant = 29.

3 × 3 Determinant — Expanding by the First Row

A 3 × 3 determinant is found by expanding with the elements of the first row. The pattern of signs is +, -, +: each element is multiplied by its minor determinant (the 2 × 2 determinant left after removing its row and column).

Example: Find the value of |3 -3 -4; 4 1 -5; 0 -1 -4|.

Step 1: First element 3: 3 × (1×(-4) - (-5)×(-1)) = 3 × (-4 - 5) = 3 × (-9) = -27.

Step 2: Second element -3 (the sign will be negative): -(-3) × (4×(-4) - (-5)×0) = 3 × (-16 - 0) = -48.

Step 3: Third element -4: (-4) × (4×(-1) - 1×0) = (-4) × (-4) = 16.

Step 4: Add all: -27 - 48 + 16 = -59.

Special property: If all the elements of a row or a column are zero, the determinant is zero. For example, in |0 a b; 0 c d; 0 x y| the whole first column is zero, so the determinant = 0.

Minor and Cofactor

The minor Mij of an element aij is the determinant which remains after removing the row and column of that element. The cofactor Aij is obtained by taking the minor with its sign:

Aij = (-1)^(i+j) × Mij

Example: For A = [2 1 1; 1 1 1; 1 -1 2], find M12, A12, M21, A21, M22, A22.

Step 1: For M12 remove the first row and second column: M12 = |1 1; 1 2| = 2 - 1 = 1.

Step 2: A12 = (-1)^(1+2) × 1 = -1.

Step 3: For M21 remove the second row and first column: M21 = |1 1; -1 2| = 2 + 1 = 3.

Step 4: A21 = (-1)^(2+1) × 3 = -3.

Step 5: M22 = |2 1; 1 2| = 4 - 1 = 3 and A22 = (-1)^(2+2) × 3 = 3.

Singular and Non-Singular Matrices

|A| = 0 ⟹ A is a singular matrix

|A| ≠ 0 ⟹ A is a non-singular matrix

Example: For what value of x will [5-x x+1; 2 4] be a singular matrix?

Step 1: Find the determinant: 4(5 - x) - 2(x + 1) = 20 - 4x - 2x - 2 = 18 - 6x.

Step 2: For singular, put the determinant equal to zero: 18 - 6x = 0.

Step 3: Solve: 6x = 18, so x = 3.

Adjoint

By forming the matrix of all the cofactors of a matrix and taking its transpose, we get the adjoint, written adj(A). An easy way for a 2 × 2 matrix: interchange the diagonal elements and change the signs of the other elements:

A = [a b; c d] ⟹ adj(A) = [d -b; -c a]

Example: For A = [1 6; 4 7], adj(A) = [7 -6; -4 1]. An important property:

A (adj A) = |A| I

Multiplicative Inverse

The multiplicative inverse of a non-singular matrix is found by this formula:

A⁻¹ = adj(A) / |A|, when |A| ≠ 0

A singular matrix (|A| = 0) has no multiplicative inverse.

Example: Find the inverse of A = [3 2; -2 -1].

Step 1: Determinant: |A| = 3×(-1) - 2×(-2) = -3 + 4 = 1.

Step 2: Adjoint: adj(A) = [-1 -2; 2 3].

Step 3: A⁻¹ = (1/1) × [-1 -2; 2 3] = [-1 -2; 2 3].

Another example: For B = [3 6; 5 10], |B| = 30 - 30 = 0, so B is singular and its multiplicative inverse does not exist.

Solving Equations — Cramer's Rule and the Inverse Method

Two equations in two unknowns can be solved by matrices. In Cramer's rule:

x = Dx / D and y = Dy / D

where D is the determinant of the coefficient matrix, and in Dx, Dy the related column is replaced by the constant terms. In the inverse method, X = A⁻¹B is used.

Example: Solve 2x + 3y = 14 and -4x + y = 28.

Step 1: D = |2 3; -4 1| = 2×1 - 3×(-4) = 2 + 12 = 14.

Step 2: Dx = |14 3; 28 1| = 14×1 - 3×28 = 14 - 84 = -70, so x = -70 / 14 = -5.

Step 3: Dy = |2 14; -4 28| = 2×28 - 14×(-4) = 56 + 56 = 112, so y = 112 / 14 = 8.

Step 4: Solution set = {(-5, 8)}.

mcqs.q: For a 2 × 2 matrix A = [a b; c d], the determinant |A| is:
mcqs.why: For a 2 × 2 matrix, |A| = ad − bc: the product of the main diagonal minus the product of the other diagonal. A determinant exists only for a square matrix, and is a single number associated with it.

mcqs.q: The value of the determinant |−5 −3; 3 −4| is:
mcqs.why: Apply |A| = ad − bc: (−5)(−4) − (−3)(3) = 20 − (−9) = 20 + 9 = 29. The double negative in the second product is the common place to slip, and it makes the answer larger, not smaller.

mcqs.q: Expanding a 3 × 3 determinant by the first row, the pattern of signs is:
mcqs.why: A 3 × 3 determinant is expanded with the elements of the first row with the sign pattern +, −, +: each element is multiplied by its minor determinant. In the worked example this gives −27 − 48 + 16 = −59.

mcqs.q: If all the elements of a row or a column of a determinant are zero, the determinant is:
mcqs.why: The notes state this special property: if all elements of a row or a column are zero, the determinant is zero. For example, in |0 a b; 0 c d; 0 x y| the whole first column is zero, so the value is 0.

mcqs.q: The cofactor Aij of an element is obtained from its minor Mij by:
mcqs.why: The cofactor is the minor with its sign: Aij = (−1)^(i+j) × Mij, where the minor is the determinant left after removing the element's row and column. For instance A12 = −M12 while A22 = +M22.

mcqs.q: A matrix A is called singular when:
mcqs.why: If |A| = 0, A is a singular matrix, and if |A| ≠ 0 it is non-singular. A singular matrix has no multiplicative inverse, which is why the value of the determinant decides whether an inverse can be found.

mcqs.q: For [5 − x, x + 1; 2, 4] to be singular, x equals:
mcqs.why: The determinant is 4(5 − x) − 2(x + 1) = 18 − 6x. For a singular matrix this must be zero: 18 − 6x = 0, so 6x = 18 and x = 3, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: The multiplicative inverse of a non-singular matrix is:
mcqs.why: The inverse is A⁻¹ = adj(A) / |A|, valid when |A| ≠ 0. For A = [3 2; −2 −1], |A| = 1 and adj(A) = [−1 −2; 2 3], so A⁻¹ is the same matrix [−1 −2; 2 3].

mcqs.q: For B = [3 6; 5 10], the multiplicative inverse:
mcqs.why: |B| = 3 × 10 − 6 × 5 = 30 − 30 = 0, so B is singular. A singular matrix has no multiplicative inverse, because the formula A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A| would require dividing by zero.

mcqs.q: By Cramer's rule, x and y are found as:
options: x = Dx / D, y = Dy / D
x = Dx × D, y = Dy × D
mcqs.why: In Cramer's rule, x = Dx / D and y = Dy / D, where D is the determinant of the coefficient matrix and in Dx, Dy the related column is replaced by the constant terms. For the worked system this gives x = −5 and y = 8.

lessons.title: Exercise 20.1 — Discriminant and the Nature of Roots
lessons.notes_html:
Quadratic Equation and Discriminant

The general form of a quadratic equation is ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0. The quantity which tells the nature of its roots is called the discriminant:

Δ = b² - 4ac

The same discriminant is also used in the quadratic formula:

x = [-b ± √(b² - 4ac)] / 2a

Nature of Roots — from the Value of Δ

Δ > 0 ⟹ two distinct real roots

Δ = 0 ⟹ two equal real roots

Δ < 0 ⟹ complex (non-real) roots

If Δ > 0 and is a perfect square, the roots are rational, and if Δ > 0 but is not a perfect square, the roots are irrational.

Example 1: Find the nature of the roots of x² + 5x - 6 = 0.

Step 1: Identify a = 1, b = 5, c = -6.

Step 2: Δ = b² - 4ac = 25 - 4(1)(-6) = 25 + 24 = 49.

Step 3: Δ = 49 > 0 and 49 = 7² is a perfect square.

Step 4: So the roots are real, rational and unequal.

Example 2: Find the nature of the roots of 1 + 6x + 9x² = 0.

Step 1: Arrange: 9x² + 6x + 1 = 0, that is, a = 9, b = 6, c = 1.

Step 2: Δ = 36 - 4(9)(1) = 36 - 36 = 0.

Step 3: Δ = 0, so the roots are real, rational and equal (both roots are -1/3).

Example 3: Find the nature of the roots of 2x² + 8 = 6x.

Step 1: Arrange: 2x² - 6x + 8 = 0, that is, a = 2, b = -6, c = 8.

Step 2: Δ = 36 - 4(2)(8) = 36 - 64 = -28.

Step 3: Δ < 0, so the roots are complex (non-real).

Value of k — for Equal or Distinct Roots

When there is an unknown coefficient (such as k) in the equation, the condition Δ = 0 is applied for equal roots and Δ > 0 for distinct real roots.

Example: For x² - 3x + k = 0, find k.

Step 1: Find Δ = 9 - 4k.

Step 2: For equal roots put Δ = 0: 9 - 4k = 0, so k = 9/4.

Step 3: For distinct real roots put Δ > 0: 9 - 4k > 0, so k < 9/4.

Another example: In x² + kx + 4 = 0, Δ = k² - 16. For equal roots k² = 16, that is, k = ±4; for distinct real roots k > 4 or k < -4.

Proofs that Roots are Real or Rational

In some equations Δ is written in the form of a sum of squares or a perfect square to show that the roots are real or rational. For example, expanding (x - a)(x - b) + (x - b)(x - c) + (x - c)(x - a) = 0 gives 3x² - 2(a + b + c)x + (ab + bc + ca) = 0, and its Δ = 2[(a - b)² + (b - c)² + (c - a)²] ≥ 0, so the roots are always real, and they are equal only when a = b = c.

mcqs.q: The discriminant of ax² + bx + c = 0 is:
mcqs.why: The discriminant is Δ = b² − 4ac, the quantity under the root in the quadratic formula x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a. Its sign alone tells the nature of the roots before solving.

mcqs.q: If Δ > 0, the roots of the quadratic equation are:
mcqs.why: The notes give the three cases: Δ > 0 means two distinct real roots, Δ = 0 means two equal real roots, and Δ < 0 means complex (non-real) roots. A positive discriminant is the case here.

mcqs.q: If Δ = 0, the roots are:
options: One root only, the other missing
mcqs.why: When Δ = 0, both roots coincide: two equal real roots. For 9x² + 6x + 1 = 0, Δ = 36 − 36 = 0 and both roots are −1/3, as the worked example shows.

mcqs.q: For x² + 5x − 6 = 0, the discriminant is:
mcqs.why: Here a = 1, b = 5, c = −6, so Δ = 25 − 4(1)(−6) = 25 + 24 = 49. Since 49 > 0 and 49 = 7² is a perfect square, the roots are real, rational and unequal.

mcqs.q: If Δ > 0 but is not a perfect square, the roots are:
mcqs.why: If Δ > 0 and is a perfect square, the roots are rational; if Δ > 0 but is not a perfect square, the roots are irrational, because the square root in the quadratic formula cannot be simplified to a rational number.

mcqs.q: For 2x² − 6x + 8 = 0, the nature of the roots is:
mcqs.why: Δ = (−6)² − 4(2)(8) = 36 − 64 = −28. A negative discriminant means the roots are complex (non-real), since the square root of a negative number is not real. The equation came from 2x² + 8 = 6x after rearranging.

mcqs.q: For x² − 3x + k = 0 to have equal roots, k must be:
mcqs.why: Δ = 9 − 4k. For equal roots put Δ = 0: 9 − 4k = 0, so k = 9/4. For distinct real roots instead, Δ > 0 gives 9 − 4k > 0, that is, k < 9/4. The condition chosen depends on the nature required.

mcqs.q: In x² + kx + 4 = 0, the values of k for equal roots are:
mcqs.why: Here Δ = k² − 16. For equal roots, k² − 16 = 0, so k² = 16 and k = ±4. For distinct real roots we would need k > 4 or k < −4, making Δ positive.

mcqs.q: In the quadratic formula, the part under the square root is:
mcqs.why: The quadratic formula is x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a, and the expression under the root, b² − 4ac, is exactly the discriminant Δ. That is why the sign of Δ decides whether the roots are real or complex.

mcqs.q: For the equation from (x − a)(x − b) + (x − b)(x − c) + (x − c)(x − a) = 0, Δ = 2[(a − b)² + (b − c)² + (c − a)²], so its roots are:
mcqs.why: Each term (a − b)², (b − c)², (c − a)² is a square, hence non-negative, so Δ ≥ 0 always and the roots are always real. They are equal only in the special case a = b = c, when Δ = 0.

lessons.title: Exercise 20.2 — Cube Roots of Unity and Properties of ω
lessons.notes_html:
Cube Roots of Unity

The number 1 has three cube roots. From x³ = 1 we get x³ - 1 = 0, which can be written as:

(x - 1)(x² + x + 1) = 0

From the first factor we get x = 1. The roots of the second factor x² + x + 1 = 0 are complex, and they are denoted by ω and ω²:

ω = (-1 + i√3) / 2 and ω² = (-1 - i√3) / 2

So the cube roots of 1 are: 1, ω and ω².

Basic Properties of ω

1 + ω + ω² = 0

ω³ = 1

From these two properties other easy forms follow:

1 + ω = -ω², 1 + ω² = -ω, ω + ω² = -1

And big powers can be reduced, because ω³ = 1: for example ω⁴ = ω³ × ω = ω and ω⁶ = 1.

Cube Roots of Any Number

If the real cube root of a number is r, then its three cube roots are r, rω and rω².

Example: Find the cube roots of 64.

Step 1: Find the real cube root of 64: 4, because 4³ = 64.

Step 2: Multiply it by 1, ω and ω².

Step 3: So the cube roots of 64 are: 4, 4ω and 4ω².

In the same way, the cube roots of 216 are 6, 6ω, 6ω², and the cube roots of -125 are -5, -5ω, -5ω² (because (-5)³ = -125).

Calculation with ω — Examples

Example 1: Find the value of (1 + ω²)⁴.

Step 1: By the property, 1 + ω² = -ω.

Step 2: (1 + ω²)⁴ = (-ω)⁴ = ω⁴.

Step 3: ω⁴ = ω³ × ω = 1 × ω = ω.

Step 4: So the answer = ω.

Example 2: Find the value of (1 - ω + ω²)(1 + ω - ω²).

Step 1: From 1 + ω² = -ω, 1 - ω + ω² = -ω - ω = -2ω.

Step 2: From 1 + ω = -ω², 1 + ω - ω² = -ω² - ω² = -2ω².

Step 3: Multiply: (-2ω)(-2ω²) = 4ω³ = 4 × 1 = 4.

Example 3: Find the value of (2 + 5ω + 2ω²)⁶.

Step 1: 2 + 5ω + 2ω² = 2(1 + ω²) + 5ω = 2(-ω) + 5ω = 3ω.

Step 2: (3ω)⁶ = 729 × ω⁶ = 729 × 1 = 729.

mcqs.q: The three cube roots of unity are:
mcqs.why: From x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) = 0, the first factor gives x = 1 and the second gives the two complex roots denoted ω and ω². So the cube roots of 1 are 1, ω and ω².

mcqs.q: The value of ω is:
mcqs.why: Solving x² + x + 1 = 0 gives ω = (−1 + i√3)/2 and ω² = (−1 − i√3)/2. The two are conjugates of each other, and ω² is literally the square of ω.

mcqs.q: Which property of ω is correct?
mcqs.why: The two basic properties are 1 + ω + ω² = 0 and ω³ = 1. From the first follow 1 + ω = −ω², 1 + ω² = −ω and ω + ω² = −1, which are used constantly in these calculations.

mcqs.q: The value of ω⁴ is:
mcqs.why: Since ω³ = 1, big powers reduce: ω⁴ = ω³ × ω = 1 × ω = ω. In the same way ω⁶ = (ω³)² = 1. Reducing the power modulo 3 is the whole trick in these questions.

mcqs.q: The cube roots of 64 are:
mcqs.why: If the real cube root of a number is r, its three cube roots are r, rω and rω². The real cube root of 64 is 4, since 4³ = 64, so the cube roots of 64 are 4, 4ω and 4ω².

mcqs.q: The value of (1 + ω²)⁴ is:
mcqs.why: By the property, 1 + ω² = −ω, so (1 + ω²)⁴ = (−ω)⁴ = ω⁴ = ω³ × ω = ω. Replacing 1 + ω² by −ω first is what makes the power easy to evaluate.

mcqs.q: The value of (1 − ω + ω²)(1 + ω − ω²) is:
mcqs.why: 1 − ω + ω² = (1 + ω²) − ω = −ω − ω = −2ω, and 1 + ω − ω² = −ω² − ω² = −2ω². Their product is (−2ω)(−2ω²) = 4ω³ = 4 × 1 = 4.

mcqs.q: The value of (2 + 5ω + 2ω²)⁶ is:
mcqs.why: Simplify inside first: 2 + 5ω + 2ω² = 2(1 + ω²) + 5ω = 2(−ω) + 5ω = 3ω. Then (3ω)⁶ = 729 ω⁶ = 729 × 1 = 729, using ω³ = 1 so ω⁶ = 1.

mcqs.q: From 1 + ω + ω² = 0, we get 1 + ω equal to:
mcqs.why: Moving ω² to the other side of 1 + ω + ω² = 0 gives 1 + ω = −ω². Similarly 1 + ω² = −ω and ω + ω² = −1; these three short forms come from the same single property.

mcqs.q: The cube roots of −125 are:
mcqs.why: The real cube root of −125 is −5, because (−5)³ = −125. Multiplying by 1, ω and ω² gives all three cube roots: −5, −5ω and −5ω², by the same rule used for 64 and 216 in the notes.

lessons.title: Exercise 20.3 — Sum and Product of Roots
lessons.notes_html:
Sum and Product of Roots

If α and β are the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0, then their sum and product are obtained directly from the coefficients:

α + β = -b / a

αβ = c / a

Example 1: Find the sum and product of the roots of x² - x - 1 = 0.

Step 1: Identify a = 1, b = -1, c = -1.

Step 2: Sum = -b/a = -(-1)/1 = 1.

Step 3: Product = c/a = -1/1 = -1.

Example 2: For 2x² - 3x - 4 = 0, a = 2, b = -3, c = -4, so the sum = 3/2 and the product = -2.

Finding an Unknown Value from the Sum and Product

When a condition is given between the sum and the product, write the formulas of both, form the equation of the condition and solve it.

Example: If the sum of the roots of x² + (3m - 7)x + 5m = 0 is 3/2 times its product, find m.

Step 1: Sum = -(3m - 7) = 7 - 3m and product = 5m.

Step 2: Apply the condition: 7 - 3m = (3/2)(5m).

Step 3: Multiply both sides by 2: 14 - 6m = 15m.

Step 4: 14 = 21m, so m = 2/3.

Sum of the Squares of the Roots

α² + β² = (α + β)² - 2αβ

Example: If the sum of the squares of the roots of x² - px + 6 = 0 is 13, find p.

Step 1: α + β = p and αβ = 6.

Step 2: α² + β² = p² - 2(6) = p² - 12.

Step 3: By the condition p² - 12 = 13, that is, p² = 25.

Step 4: So p = ±5.

Difference of the Roots

(α - β)² = (α + β)² - 4αβ

Example: If the roots of x² - 5x + 2m = 0 differ by 1, find m.

Step 1: α + β = 5 and αβ = 2m.

Step 2: (α - β)² = 25 - 8m.

Step 3: The difference is 1, so (α - β)² = 1, that is, 25 - 8m = 1.

Step 4: 8m = 24, so m = 3.

mcqs.q: If α, β are the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0, then α + β equals:
mcqs.why: The sum of the roots is α + β = −b/a, with the negative sign, and the product is αβ = c/a. For x² − x − 1 = 0 this gives sum = −(−1)/1 = 1 and product = −1.

mcqs.q: For 2x² − 3x − 4 = 0, the sum and product of the roots are:
mcqs.why: Here a = 2, b = −3, c = −4. Sum = −b/a = 3/2 and product = c/a = −4/2 = −2. Reading a, b, c with their signs correctly is the key step in every such question.

mcqs.q: The identity for the sum of the squares of the roots is:
mcqs.why: Expanding (α + β)² = α² + 2αβ + β² and rearranging gives α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ. The notes use it to find p = ±5 when the sum of squares for x² − px + 6 = 0 is 13.

mcqs.q: If the sum of the squares of the roots of x² − px + 6 = 0 is 13, then p is:
mcqs.why: Here α + β = p and αβ = 6, so α² + β² = p² − 12. Setting p² − 12 = 13 gives p² = 25, hence p = ±5. Both signs work because only p² appears in the condition.

mcqs.q: The formula for (α − β)² in terms of the sum and product is:
mcqs.why: (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ. For x² − 5x + 2m = 0 this gives 25 − 8m; when the roots differ by 1, 25 − 8m = 1 gives m = 3, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: If the roots of x² − 5x + 2m = 0 differ by 1, then m equals:
mcqs.why: α + β = 5 and αβ = 2m, so (α − β)² = 25 − 8m. The difference is 1, so (α − β)² = 1: 25 − 8m = 1 gives 8m = 24 and m = 3. Squaring the difference first is the standard device.

mcqs.q: If the sum of the roots of x² + (3m − 7)x + 5m = 0 is 3/2 times its product, then m is:
mcqs.why: Sum = −(3m − 7) = 7 − 3m and product = 5m. The condition gives 7 − 3m = (3/2)(5m); multiplying by 2, 14 − 6m = 15m, so 14 = 21m and m = 2/3.

mcqs.q: For x² − x − 1 = 0, the product of the roots is:
mcqs.why: The product is αβ = c/a = −1/1 = −1, while the sum is −b/a = 1. Notice the product takes the sign of c, which is negative here, so the two roots have opposite signs.

mcqs.q: Which condition is set up using α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ?
options: A condition on the sum of the squares of the roots
mcqs.why: Whenever a condition speaks of α² + β², we rewrite it through the sum and product: α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ. This converts the condition into an equation in the unknown coefficient, like p² − 12 = 13.

mcqs.q: For the equation ax² + bx + c = 0, the product αβ is:
mcqs.why: The product of the roots is αβ = c/a, the constant term divided by the coefficient of x². Together with α + β = −b/a, these two formulas answer almost every question of this exercise.

lessons.title: Exercise 20.4 — Symmetric Functions of Roots
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Symmetric Function?

A symmetric function of the roots is a function which does not change when the places of α and β are interchanged, that is, f(α, β) = f(β, α). For example α + β, αβ and α² + β² are symmetric functions, but α - β is not symmetric.

Every symmetric function can be written in the form of α + β and αβ, and then its value is found from the coefficients of the equation.

Important Identities

α² + β² = (α + β)² - 2αβ

(α - β)² = (α + β)² - 4αβ

α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ - 3αβ(α + β)

1/α + 1/β = (α + β) / (αβ)

More forms are also made from these, such as α³β + αβ³ = αβ[(α + β)² - 2αβ] and 1/α³ + 1/β³ = [(α + β)³ - 3αβ(α + β)] / (αβ)³.

Example — Values for a Given Equation

Example: α and β are the roots of 2x² - 3x + 7 = 0; find the value of (1/α + 1/β)².

Step 1: From the coefficients, α + β = 3/2 and αβ = 7/2.

Step 2: 1/α + 1/β = (α + β) / (αβ) = (3/2) / (7/2) = 3/7.

Step 3: Square: (3/7)² = 9/49.

Step 4: So (1/α + 1/β)² = 9/49.

Another example: For the same equation α/β² + β/α² = (α³ + β³) / (αβ)². α³ + β³ = (3/2)³ - 3(7/2)(3/2) = 27/8 - 63/4 = -99/8 and (αβ)² = 49/4, so the answer = (-99/8) / (49/4) = -99/98.

Another Pattern

Example: α and β are the roots of px² + qx + q = 0 (p ≠ 0); find √(α/β) + √(β/α).

Step 1: α + β = -q/p and αβ = q/p.

Step 2: Write √(α/β) + √(β/α) = (α + β) / √(αβ).

Step 3: Put the values: (-q/p) / √(q/p) = -√(q/p).

Step 4: So the answer = -√(q/p).

Remember: A symmetric equation such as α + β = 8 represents a straight line in the (α, β) plane, which passes through (0, 8) and (8, 0).

mcqs.q: A symmetric function of α and β is one which:
options: Changes sign when α and β are interchanged
Does not change when α and β are interchanged
mcqs.why: A symmetric function does not change when the places of α and β are interchanged: f(α, β) = f(β, α). Examples are α + β, αβ and α² + β², while α − β is not symmetric because swapping changes its sign.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT a symmetric function of the roots?
mcqs.why: α − β becomes β − α = −(α − β) when the roots are swapped, so it changes and is not symmetric. The others, α + β, αβ and α² + β², are listed in the notes as symmetric functions.

mcqs.q: 1/α + 1/β can be written as:
mcqs.why: Taking the common denominator αβ: 1/α + 1/β = (β + α)/(αβ) = (α + β)/(αβ). Every symmetric function can be written using α + β and αβ, and then valued from the coefficients.

mcqs.q: α³ + β³ equals:
mcqs.why: The identity is α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β). For 2x² − 3x + 7 = 0 it gives α³ + β³ = 27/8 − 63/4 = −99/8, used in the second worked example of the lesson.

mcqs.q: For 2x² − 3x + 7 = 0, the value of (1/α + 1/β)² is:
mcqs.why: α + β = 3/2 and αβ = 7/2, so 1/α + 1/β = (3/2)/(7/2) = 3/7. Squaring gives (3/7)² = 9/49. The inner value 3/7 itself is only the unsquared step, so the answer is 9/49.

mcqs.q: For the same equation, α/β² + β/α² equals:
mcqs.why: α/β² + β/α² = (α³ + β³)/(αβ)². With α³ + β³ = −99/8 and (αβ)² = 49/4, the value is (−99/8)/(49/4) = −99/98. Both the sum of cubes and the square of the product come from α + β and αβ.

mcqs.q: For px² + qx + q = 0, √(α/β) + √(β/α) equals:
