mcqs.why: α + β = −q/p and αβ = q/p. Writing √(α/β) + √(β/α) = (α + β)/√(αβ) gives (−q/p)/√(q/p) = −√(q/p). The negative sign survives from α + β = −q/p, so the answer is negative.

mcqs.q: α³β + αβ³ can be written as:
mcqs.why: Factor out αβ: α³β + αβ³ = αβ(α² + β²) = αβ[(α + β)² − 2αβ], using the sum-of-squares identity. The notes list this among the forms built from the basic identities.

mcqs.q: The equation α + β = 8 in the (α, β) plane represents:
mcqs.why: The notes remark that a symmetric equation such as α + β = 8 represents a straight line in the (α, β) plane, passing through (0, 8) and (8, 0). It is a line because it is a first-degree relation between α and β.

mcqs.q: To find the value of a symmetric function, we first express it in terms of:
mcqs.why: Every symmetric function can be written in the form of α + β and αβ, and then its value is found from the coefficients of the equation, since α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. This is the method of the whole lesson.

lessons.title: Exercise 20.5 — Forming Equations from Given Roots and Conditions for One Root
lessons.notes_html:
Forming an Equation from Given Roots

If the roots of a quadratic equation are α and β, then the equation is written in this form:

x² - (α + β)x + αβ = 0

Example 1: Form the equation whose roots are 2 and -3.

Step 1: Sum = 2 + (-3) = -1.

Step 2: Product = 2 × (-3) = -6.

Step 3: Put in the formula: x² - (-1)x + (-6) = 0.

Step 4: So the equation is: x² + x - 6 = 0.

Example 2: For the roots 2 + i and 2 - i, the sum = 4 and the product = (2 + i)(2 - i) = 4 + 1 = 5, so the equation is x² - 4x + 5 = 0. In the same way, for ω and ω² the sum = -1 and the product = 1, so the equation is x² + x + 1 = 0.

New Equations with Changed Roots

Method: From the sum and product of the old roots, find the sum and product of the new roots, then apply the same formula.

Example: α and β are the roots of 6x² - 3x + 1 = 0. Form the equation whose roots are 1/α and 1/β.

Step 1: Old sum and product: α + β = 3/6 = 1/2 and αβ = 1/6.

Step 2: New sum = 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/(αβ) = (1/2)/(1/6) = 3.

Step 3: New product = 1/(αβ) = 6.

Step 4: So the new equation is: x² - 3x + 6 = 0.

Remember the general forms:

Equation for the reciprocals of the roots of px² - qx + r = 0: rx² - qx + p = 0

Equation for the doubles of the roots of x² - px + q = 0: x² - 2px + 4q = 0

The equation for the squares of the roots (α², β²) of the same equation 6x² - 3x + 1 = 0 is 36x² + 3x + 1 = 0, because the new sum = (α + β)² - 2αβ = 1/4 - 1/3 = -1/12 and the new product = (αβ)² = 1/36.

Conditions about One Root

Famous conditions about one root of ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0):

One root is the negative of the other, that is, β = -α ⟹ b = 0

One root is the reciprocal of the other, that is, β = 1/α ⟹ c = a

Reason for the first condition: if β = -α, the sum of the roots becomes zero, and the sum = -b/a, so b = 0. Reason for the second condition: if β = 1/α, the product becomes 1, and the product = c/a, so c = a. The condition for one root being the square of the other is longer: b³ + ac² - 3abc + a²c = 0.

mcqs.q: The equation with roots α and β is written as:
mcqs.why: If the roots are α and β, the equation is x² − (sum)x + (product) = 0, that is, x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0. The minus sign belongs with the sum, which is the most common slip in this exercise.

mcqs.q: The equation whose roots are 2 and −3 is:
mcqs.why: Sum = 2 + (−3) = −1 and product = 2 × (−3) = −6. Putting these in x² − (sum)x + product = 0 gives x² − (−1)x − 6 = x² + x − 6 = 0, as in the first worked example.

mcqs.q: The equation whose roots are 2 + i and 2 − i is:
mcqs.why: Sum = (2 + i) + (2 − i) = 4 and product = (2 + i)(2 − i) = 4 + 1 = 5. So the equation is x² − 4x + 5 = 0. Complex roots of a real equation occur in such conjugate pairs.

mcqs.q: The equation whose roots are ω and ω² is:
mcqs.why: For ω and ω², the sum is ω + ω² = −1 and the product is ω × ω² = ω³ = 1. Hence the equation is x² − (−1)x + 1 = x² + x + 1 = 0, the same factor that produced ω in the earlier lesson.

mcqs.q: α, β are roots of 6x² − 3x + 1 = 0. The equation with roots 1/α and 1/β is:
mcqs.why: Old sum = 1/2 and old product = 1/6. New sum = (α + β)/(αβ) = (1/2)/(1/6) = 3 and new product = 1/(αβ) = 6. So the new equation is x² − 3x + 6 = 0, by the standard method for changed roots.

mcqs.q: If one root of ax² + bx + c = 0 is the negative of the other, then:
mcqs.why: If β = −α, the sum of the roots is zero, and the sum equals −b/a, so b = 0. The reason is given in the notes: the sum vanishing forces the coefficient of x to vanish.

mcqs.q: If one root is the reciprocal of the other, then:
mcqs.why: If β = 1/α, the product αβ becomes 1, and the product equals c/a, so c/a = 1, that is, c = a. This is the famous reciprocal-root condition listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: The equation for the reciprocals of the roots of px² − qx + r = 0 is:
mcqs.why: The general form given in the notes: the equation for the reciprocals of the roots of px² − qx + r = 0 is rx² − qx + p = 0 — the first and last coefficients change places while the middle one stays.

mcqs.q: The equation for the doubles of the roots of x² − px + q = 0 is:
mcqs.why: Doubling both roots doubles the sum and multiplies the product by 4. The notes give the result directly: for x² − px + q = 0, the doubles of the roots satisfy x² − 2px + 4q = 0.

mcqs.q: For 6x² − 3x + 1 = 0, the equation with roots α² and β² is:
mcqs.why: New sum = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 1/4 − 1/3 = −1/12 and new product = (αβ)² = 1/36. Clearing fractions, the equation is 36x² + 3x + 1 = 0, as stated in the notes; note the plus sign from the negative sum.

lessons.title: Exercise 20.6 — Roots of Cubic and Biquadratic Equations by Synthetic Division
lessons.notes_html:
Synthetic Division

If one root of a cubic or higher-degree equation is known, the remaining roots can be found by synthetic division. The method is: perform synthetic division on the coefficients of the equation with the given root k; the quotient obtained is an equation of one degree less; by solving it, the remaining roots are found. If the given root is correct, the last remainder always comes out zero.

Example: One root of x³ - 4x² + x + 6 = 0 is x = 3; find the remaining roots.

Step 1: Write the coefficients: 1, -4, 1, 6. The dividing number is k = 3.

Step 2: Bring the first coefficient 1 straight down.

Step 3: 1 × 3 = 3; write it under -4 and add: -4 + 3 = -1.

Step 4: -1 × 3 = -3; write it under 1 and add: 1 + (-3) = -2.

Step 5: -2 × 3 = -6; write it under 6 and add: 6 + (-6) = 0. The remainder is zero, so 3 is really a root.

Step 6: The coefficients of the quotient are 1, -1, -2, that is, the quotient = x² - x - 2 = 0.

Step 7: Factorise: (x - 2)(x + 1) = 0.

Step 8: So the remaining roots are: 2 and -1.

More Examples of Cubic Equations

In 2x³ - x² - 2x + 1 = 0, x = 1 is given. By synthetic division the quotient 2x² + x - 1 = 0 is obtained, that is, (2x - 1)(x + 1) = 0, so the remaining roots are 1/2 and -1. In the same way, if in x³ - 28x + 48 = 0, x = 2 is given, the quotient x² + 2x - 24 = (x + 6)(x - 4) is obtained and the remaining roots are -6 and 4.

Biquadratic Equation

In a biquadratic (fourth-degree) equation, if two roots are given, synthetic division is done twice and in the end a quadratic quotient remains. For example, in x⁴ + 2x³ - 13x² - 14x + 24 = 0 the roots 3 and -4 are given; after dividing twice, the quotient x² + x - 2 = (x + 2)(x - 1) is obtained, so the remaining roots are -2 and 1.

Some biquadratic equations contain only powers of x². Example: In x⁴ + 4x² - 5 = 0, put x² = y:

Step 1: y² + 4y - 5 = 0 is formed.

Step 2: Factorise: (y + 5)(y - 1) = 0, that is, y = 1 or y = -5.

Step 3: From y = 1, x = ±1 (these are the given roots).

Step 4: From y = -5, x² = -5, that is, x = ±i√5.

Step 5: So the remaining roots are: i√5 and -i√5.

Finding an Unknown Coefficient from a Given Root

If there is an unknown coefficient in the equation and one root is given, then putting that root in the equation gives the coefficient, because a root satisfies the equation.

Example: One root of x³ - 3ax² - x + 6 = 0 is 1; find a and the remaining roots.

Step 1: Put x = 1: 1 - 3a - 1 + 6 = 0, that is, 6 - 3a = 0.

Step 2: So a = 2.

Step 3: Now the equation is x³ - 6x² - x + 6 = 0; synthetic division with x = 1 gives the quotient x² - 5x - 6.

Step 4: Factorise: (x - 6)(x + 1) = 0.

Step 5: So the remaining roots are: 6 and -1.

mcqs.q: In synthetic division, if the given number really is a root, the final remainder is:
mcqs.why: If the given root is correct, the last remainder in synthetic division always comes out zero. A non-zero remainder would show that the number is not actually a root of the equation.

mcqs.q: One root of x³ − 4x² + x + 6 = 0 is 3. The quotient after synthetic division is:
mcqs.why: Dividing the coefficients 1, −4, 1, 6 by 3 gives quotient coefficients 1, −1, −2 with remainder 0, so the quotient is x² − x − 2 = 0. Factorising, (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0, giving the remaining roots 2 and −1.

mcqs.q: For that cubic, the remaining roots besides 3 are:
mcqs.why: The quotient x² − x − 2 factorises as (x − 2)(x + 1), so x = 2 or x = −1. Together with the given root 3, the cubic x³ − 4x² + x + 6 = 0 has roots 3, 2 and −1.

mcqs.q: In 2x³ − x² − 2x + 1 = 0 with given root 1, the remaining roots are:
mcqs.why: Synthetic division with x = 1 gives the quotient 2x² + x − 1 = 0, which factorises as (2x − 1)(x + 1) = 0. Hence the remaining roots are 1/2 and −1, as the notes record.

mcqs.q: In x³ − 28x + 48 = 0 with given root 2, the quotient is:
mcqs.why: Synthetic division by 2 on the coefficients 1, 0, −28, 48 gives the quotient x² + 2x − 24, which factorises as (x + 6)(x − 4). So the remaining roots are −6 and 4, besides the given root 2.

mcqs.q: For the biquadratic x⁴ + 2x³ − 13x² − 14x + 24 = 0 with given roots 3 and −4, the remaining roots are:
mcqs.why: In a biquadratic with two given roots, synthetic division is done twice, leaving the quadratic quotient x² + x − 2 = (x + 2)(x − 1). So the remaining roots are −2 and 1, completing the four roots 3, −4, −2, 1.

mcqs.q: Putting x² = y in x⁴ + 4x² − 5 = 0 gives which quadratic?
mcqs.why: Some biquadratic equations contain only powers of x²; putting x² = y turns x⁴ + 4x² − 5 = 0 into y² + 4y − 5 = 0. This factorises as (y + 5)(y − 1) = 0, giving y = 1 or y = −5.

mcqs.q: From y = −5 in that equation, the corresponding roots are:
mcqs.why: y = x² = −5 gives x² = −5, so x = ±i√5. Together with x = ±1 from y = 1, the four roots are 1, −1, i√5 and −i√5; the notes list ±i√5 as the remaining roots.

mcqs.q: One root of x³ − 3ax² − x + 6 = 0 is 1. The value of a is found by:
options: Putting x = 1 in the equation, since a root satisfies it
mcqs.why: A root satisfies the equation, so putting x = 1 gives 1 − 3a − 1 + 6 = 0, that is, 6 − 3a = 0 and a = 2. Only after finding a is synthetic division used to get the remaining roots 6 and −1.

mcqs.q: With a = 2, the remaining roots of that cubic are:
mcqs.why: With a = 2 the equation is x³ − 6x² − x + 6 = 0. Synthetic division with x = 1 gives the quotient x² − 5x − 6 = (x − 6)(x + 1), so the remaining roots are 6 and −1.

lessons.title: Exercise 20.7 — Simultaneous Equations and Word Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Simultaneous Equations — Substitution Method

When one equation is linear and the other quadratic, write one unknown from the linear equation in terms of the other and put it in the quadratic equation. In this way a quadratic equation in one unknown is formed; by solving it, the values of both unknowns are found.

Example: Solve 2x - y = 3 and x² + y² = 2.

Step 1: From the first equation write y = 2x - 3.

Step 2: Put it in the second equation: x² + (2x - 3)² = 2.

Step 3: Expand and simplify: x² + 4x² - 12x + 9 = 2, that is, 5x² - 12x + 7 = 0.

Step 4: Factorise: (5x - 7)(x - 1) = 0, that is, x = 7/5 or x = 1.

Step 5: For x = 7/5, y = 2(7/5) - 3 = -1/5, and for x = 1, y = 2 - 3 = -1.

Step 6: Solution set = {(7/5, -1/5), (1, -1)}.

Two Quadratic Equations

When both equations are quadratic, often an easy form is obtained by adding or subtracting them.

Example: Solve x² + y² = 5 and xy = 2.

Step 1: (x + y)² = x² + y² + 2xy = 5 + 4 = 9, so x + y = ±3.

Step 2: (x - y)² = x² + y² - 2xy = 5 - 4 = 1, so x - y = ±1.

Step 3: Solving the pairs together gives four solutions.

Step 4: Solution set = {(2, 1), (1, 2), (-2, -1), (-1, -2)}.

Another example: Subtracting in x² + xy = 5 and x² - 2xy = 2 gives 3xy = 3, that is, xy = 1. Then from the first equation x² = 4, that is, x = ±2 and y = ±1/2 (with the same sign), so the solution set = {(2, 1/2), (-2, -1/2)}.

Word Problems

In word problems, take the unknown as x, form the equation from the condition, and then solve it in the same way.

Example: The sum of the squares of two numbers is 100 and one number is 2 more than the other; find the numbers.

Step 1: Take the numbers as x and x + 2.

Step 2: From the condition: x² + (x + 2)² = 100.

Step 3: Expand: 2x² + 4x + 4 = 100, that is, x² + 2x - 48 = 0.

Step 4: Factorise: (x + 8)(x - 6) = 0, that is, x = 6 or x = -8.

Step 5: So the numbers are (6, 8) or (-8, -6).

Another example: The difference of two numbers is 5 and the difference of their squares is 275. From x - y = 5 and x² - y² = (x - y)(x + y) = 275 we get x + y = 275/5 = 55. Solving both together gives x = 30 and y = 25.

mcqs.q: When one equation is linear and the other quadratic, the usual method is:
options: Express one unknown from the linear equation and substitute in the quadratic
mcqs.why: By substitution: write one unknown from the linear equation in terms of the other and put it in the quadratic equation. A quadratic in one unknown results, whose solutions give both unknowns.

mcqs.q: Solving 2x − y = 3 and x² + y² = 2, the quadratic formed after substitution is:
mcqs.why: From the linear equation y = 2x − 3. Putting it in x² + y² = 2 gives x² + (2x − 3)² = 2, which expands to 5x² − 12x + 7 = 0. This factorises as (5x − 7)(x − 1) = 0, giving x = 7/5 or 1.

mcqs.q: The solution set of 2x − y = 3 and x² + y² = 2 is:
mcqs.why: x = 7/5 gives y = 2(7/5) − 3 = −1/5, and x = 1 gives y = 2 − 3 = −1. So the solution set is {(7/5, −1/5), (1, −1)}; each x must be paired with its own y from the linear equation.

mcqs.q: Solving x² + y² = 5 and xy = 2, we first get:
mcqs.why: (x + y)² = x² + y² + 2xy = 5 + 4 = 9, so x + y = ±3, and (x − y)² = 5 − 4 = 1, so x − y = ±1. Solving these pairs together gives the four solutions of the system.

mcqs.q: The solution set of x² + y² = 5, xy = 2 is:
mcqs.why: Combining x + y = ±3 with x − y = ±1 in all sign choices gives four pairs: (2, 1), (1, 2), (−2, −1) and (−1, −2). Each pair indeed gives x² + y² = 5 and xy = 2, so all four belong to the solution set.

mcqs.q: Subtracting x² − 2xy = 2 from x² + xy = 5 gives:
mcqs.why: Subtracting eliminates x²: (x² + xy) − (x² − 2xy) = 5 − 2 gives 3xy = 3, so xy = 1. Then from the first equation x² = 4, x = ±2 and y = ±1/2 with the same sign.

mcqs.q: The sum of the squares of two numbers is 100 and one is 2 more than the other. The equation formed is:
mcqs.why: Take the numbers as x and x + 2: x² + (x + 2)² = 100 expands to 2x² + 4x + 4 = 100, and dividing by 2 gives x² + 2x − 48 = 0. Factorising, (x + 8)(x − 6) = 0, so x = 6 or x = −8.

mcqs.q: Those two numbers are:
mcqs.why: With x = 6 the numbers are 6 and 8; with x = −8 they are −8 and −6. Both pairs differ by 2 and their squares sum to 36 + 64 = 100 (and 64 + 36 = 100), so both are valid answers.

mcqs.q: The difference of two numbers is 5 and the difference of their squares is 275. The numbers are:
mcqs.why: From x² − y² = (x − y)(x + y) = 275 and x − y = 5, we get x + y = 275/5 = 55. Solving x − y = 5 with x + y = 55 gives x = 30 and y = 25, as in the notes.

mcqs.q: In word problems, after taking the unknown as x, the next step is to:
options: Form the equation from the given condition and solve it
mcqs.why: In word problems, take the unknown as x, form the equation from the condition, and then solve it in the same way as ordinary equations. The modelling step — turning words into an equation — is the essential part.

lessons.title: Exercise 21.1 — Non-Repeated Linear Factors and Proper and Improper Fractions
lessons.notes_html:
What are Partial Fractions?

Writing one big rational fraction as a sum of smaller simple fractions is called partial fractions. A rational fraction is the quotient of two polynomial expressions.

P(x) / Q(x), Q(x) ≠ 0

In a proper fraction the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator. In an improper fraction the degree of the numerator is equal to or greater than the degree of the denominator. An improper fraction is first divided and changed into a proper fraction.

Form for Non-Repeated Linear Factors

If all the factors of the denominator are linear and no factor repeats, a separate fraction is written for each factor.

P(x) / ((x-a)(x-b)) = A / (x-a) + B / (x-b)

An easy method to find A and B: multiply both sides by the denominator, then put the value of x which makes each factor zero. In this way only one unknown remains at a time. The remaining unknowns are found by comparison.

Example 1: Resolve 12 / (x² - 9) into partial fractions

Step 1: Factorise the denominator: x² - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3).

Step 2: Assume the form: 12 / ((x-3)(x+3)) = A / (x-3) + B / (x+3).

Step 3: Multiply both sides by (x-3)(x+3): 12 = A(x + 3) + B(x - 3).

Step 4: Put x = 3: 12 = 6A, so A = 2.

Step 5: Put x = -3: 12 = -6B, so B = -2.

Step 6: Write the answer: 12 / (x² - 9) = 2 / (x - 3) - 2 / (x + 3).

Example 2: Improper Fraction — Divide First

In (3x³ - 2x² - 16x + 20) / ((x - 2)(x + 2)) the degree of the numerator is greater, so division is done first.

Step 1: On dividing, the quotient 3x - 2 and the remainder (-4x + 12) are obtained.

Step 2: Find the partial fractions of the remaining proper fraction: (-4x + 12) / ((x-2)(x+2)) = 1 / (x - 2) - 5 / (x + 2).

Step 3: Complete answer: 3x - 2 + 1 / (x - 2) - 5 / (x + 2).

Remember: In a fraction such as (x² + 9x + 8) / (x² + x - 6) also, division first gives 1, and then the partial fractions of the remainder (8x + 14) are 2 / (x + 3) + 6 / (x - 2).

mcqs.q: Writing one rational fraction as a sum of smaller simple fractions is called:
mcqs.why: Writing one big rational fraction as a sum of smaller simple fractions is called resolving it into partial fractions. A rational fraction is the quotient P(x)/Q(x) of two polynomials, with Q(x) ≠ 0.

mcqs.q: A fraction is proper when:
options: The degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator
The numerator has the smaller degree
mcqs.why: In a proper fraction the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator. In an improper fraction the numerator's degree is equal to or greater, and then division is done first to make it proper.

mcqs.q: For non-repeated linear factors, P(x)/((x − a)(x − b)) is written as:
mcqs.why: If all the factors of the denominator are linear and none repeats, a separate fraction with a constant numerator is written for each factor: A/(x − a) + B/(x − b). The constants are found by substituting or comparing.

mcqs.q: Resolving 12/(x² − 9), the factorised denominator is:
mcqs.why: x² − 9 is a difference of squares: (x − 3)(x + 3). Only after factorising can the partial-fraction form A/(x − 3) + B/(x + 3) be assumed and the constants found.

mcqs.q: 12/(x² − 9) resolves into:
mcqs.why: From 12 = A(x + 3) + B(x − 3): putting x = 3 gives 12 = 6A, so A = 2; putting x = −3 gives 12 = −6B, so B = −2. Hence the answer is 2/(x − 3) − 2/(x + 3).

mcqs.q: The easy method to find A first in such questions is to:
options: Put the value of x which makes the factor (x − a) zero
mcqs.why: Multiply both sides by the denominator, then put the value of x which makes each factor zero. That kills the other unknown's term, leaving only one unknown at a time; the rest are found by comparison.

mcqs.q: The fraction (3x³ − 2x² − 16x + 20)/((x − 2)(x + 2)) is improper, so first we:
mcqs.why: The numerator has degree 3, greater than the denominator's degree 2, so division is done first. The quotient is 3x − 2 with remainder (−4x + 12), and only the remaining proper fraction is resolved into partial fractions.

mcqs.q: The complete resolution of that improper fraction is:
mcqs.why: The proper part (−4x + 12)/((x − 2)(x + 2)) resolves to 1/(x − 2) − 5/(x + 2). Adding the quotient gives the full answer: 3x − 2 + 1/(x − 2) − 5/(x + 2), as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: For (x² + 9x + 8)/(x² + x − 6), division first gives quotient:
mcqs.why: Both numerator and denominator have degree 2, so the fraction is improper and division gives quotient 1 with remainder 8x + 14. The remainder's partial fractions are 2/(x + 3) + 6/(x − 2), as the notes recall.

mcqs.q: A rational fraction is:
options: The quotient of two polynomial expressions, P(x)/Q(x) with Q(x) ≠ 0
A polynomial divided by a constant only
mcqs.why: A rational fraction is the quotient of two polynomial expressions, written P(x)/Q(x) with Q(x) ≠ 0. Partial fractions rewrite such a quotient as a sum of simpler fractions, one for each factor of Q(x).

lessons.title: Exercise 21.2 — Repeated Linear Factors
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Repeated Linear Factor?

If the same linear factor comes two or three times in the denominator, such as (x + 1)² or (x - 2)³, it is called a repeated factor. For such a factor, not one but as many fractions are written as the number of times the factor repeats — from power 1 up to the full power.

P(x) / (x + 1)² = A / (x + 1) + B / (x + 1)²

P(x) / (x - 2)³ = A / (x - 2) + B / (x - 2)² + C / (x - 2)³

In the method, first put the value which makes the factor zero to find the last unknown, then find the remaining unknowns by comparing the coefficients of x and x².

Example 1: Resolve (4x - 3) / (x + 1)² into partial fractions

Step 1: Write the form: (4x - 3) / (x + 1)² = A / (x + 1) + B / (x + 1)².

Step 2: Multiply both sides by (x + 1)²: 4x - 3 = A(x + 1) + B.

Step 3: Put x = -1: -4 - 3 = B, so B = -7.

Step 4: Compare the coefficient of x: 4 = A, so A = 4.

Step 5: Write the answer: 4 / (x + 1) - 7 / (x + 1)².

Example 2: Resolve (x² - x + 3) / (x - 1)³ into partial fractions

Step 1: Write the form: A / (x - 1) + B / (x - 1)² + C / (x - 1)³.

Step 2: Put x = 1: C = 1 - 1 + 3 = 3 is obtained.

Step 3: Compare the coefficient of x²: A = 1 is obtained.

Step 4: Compare the coefficient of x: B = 1 is obtained.

Step 5: Write the answer: 1 / (x - 1) + 1 / (x - 1)² + 3 / (x - 1)³.

mcqs.q: For a repeated linear factor (x + 1)², the partial-fraction form is:
mcqs.why: For a repeated factor, as many fractions are written as the number of times the factor repeats — from power 1 up to the full power. So (x + 1)² needs A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)², not a single fraction.

mcqs.q: For (x − 2)³ in the denominator, the form needs:
mcqs.why: The factor (x − 2) repeats three times, so three fractions are written, one for each power 1, 2 and 3: A/(x − 2) + B/(x − 2)² + C/(x − 2)³. Missing a power is the classic error in this lesson.

mcqs.q: Resolving (4x − 3)/(x + 1)², putting x = −1 first gives:
mcqs.why: From 4x − 3 = A(x + 1) + B, putting x = −1 removes the A term: −4 − 3 = B, so B = −7. The last unknown (for the highest power) is always found first by this substitution.

mcqs.q: In that same resolution, A is found by comparing the coefficient of x, giving:
mcqs.why: Comparing the coefficient of x on both sides of 4x − 3 = A(x + 1) + B gives 4 = A. So the resolution is 4/(x + 1) − 7/(x + 1)², with A from comparison and B from substitution.

mcqs.q: (4x − 3)/(x + 1)² resolves into:
mcqs.why: With A = 4 (from the coefficient of x) and B = −7 (from x = −1), the answer is 4/(x + 1) − 7/(x + 1)². The negative sign of B must be kept when writing the second fraction.

mcqs.q: Resolving (x² − x + 3)/(x − 1)³, putting x = 1 gives C equal to:
mcqs.why: Putting x = 1 in the numerator expression gives C = 1 − 1 + 3 = 3 directly, because the A and B terms vanish at the repeated factor's zero. Then comparison gives A = 1 and B = 1, completing the resolution.

mcqs.q: (x² − x + 3)/(x − 1)³ resolves into:
mcqs.why: Comparing coefficients gives A = 1 (from x²) and B = 1 (from x), while substitution gave C = 3. So the resolution is 1/(x − 1) + 1/(x − 1)² + 3/(x − 1)³, one fraction for each power.

mcqs.q: In the method for repeated factors, the remaining unknowns after substitution are found by:
options: Comparing the coefficients of x and x²
mcqs.why: First put the value which makes the factor zero to find the last unknown, then find the remaining unknowns by comparing the coefficients of x and x² on the two sides. Both worked examples follow exactly this order.

mcqs.q: A factor such as (x − 2)³ is called:
mcqs.why: If the same linear factor comes two or three times in the denominator, such as (x + 1)² or (x − 2)³, it is called a repeated (linear) factor. Each repetition adds one more partial fraction to the assumed form.

mcqs.q: Why must (x + 1)² have two partial fractions instead of one?
options: Because the factor repeats twice, one fraction per power
Because A and B are always two
mcqs.why: The rule of the lesson: for a repeated factor, as many fractions are written as the number of times the factor repeats — from power 1 up to the full power. (x + 1)² repeats twice, so it needs both A/(x + 1) and B/(x + 1)².

lessons.title: Exercise 21.3 — Non-Repeated Quadratic Factors
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Non-Repeated Quadratic Factor?

Some denominator factors are such that they cannot be broken further into factors in real numbers, such as x² + 7 or x² + 3. For such a quadratic factor, not just one constant but Ax + B is written in the numerator of the fraction, because the degree of the numerator should be one less than the degree of the denominator.

P(x) / ((x² + 7)(x - 2)) = (Ax + B) / (x² + 7) + C / (x - 2)

Method: First put the value which makes the linear factor zero to find C, then find A and B by comparing the coefficients of x² and x.

Example 1: Resolve (x² - x - 13) / ((x² + 7)(x - 2)) into partial fractions

Step 1: Write the form: (Ax + B) / (x² + 7) + C / (x - 2).

Step 2: Multiply both sides by (x² + 7)(x - 2): x² - x - 13 = (Ax + B)(x - 2) + C(x² + 7).

Step 3: Put x = 2: 4 - 2 - 13 = C(4 + 7), that is, -11 = 11C, so C = -1.

Step 4: Compare the coefficient of x²: 1 = A + C = A - 1, so A = 2.

Step 5: Compare the coefficient of x: -1 = -2A + B = -4 + B, so B = 3.

Step 6: Write the answer: (2x + 3) / (x² + 7) - 1 / (x - 2).

Example 2: Resolve (x² - x + 2) / ((x + 1)(x² + 3)) into partial fractions

Step 1: Write the form: A / (x + 1) + (Bx + C) / (x² + 3).

Step 2: Put x = -1: 1 + 1 + 2 = A(1 + 3), that is, 4 = 4A, so A = 1.

Step 3: Compare the coefficient of x²: B = 0 is obtained.

Step 4: Compare the coefficient of x: C = -1 is obtained.

Step 5: Write the answer: 1 / (x + 1) - 1 / (x² + 3). Here, since B = 0, only a constant remains in the quadratic fraction.

mcqs.q: For an irreducible quadratic factor such as x² + 7, the numerator of its partial fraction is written as:
mcqs.why: For a quadratic factor that cannot be broken further in real numbers, such as x² + 7 or x² + 3, the numerator is Ax + B, not just a constant, because the numerator's degree should be one less than the denominator factor's degree.

mcqs.q: In P(x)/((x² + 7)(x − 2)), the correct assumed form is:
mcqs.why: The quadratic factor x² + 7 takes the linear numerator Ax + B, and the linear factor (x − 2) takes the constant C. This pairing — linear numerator over a quadratic factor — is the rule of the lesson.

mcqs.q: Resolving (x² − x − 13)/((x² + 7)(x − 2)), putting x = 2 gives:
mcqs.why: Putting x = 2 in x² − x − 13 = (Ax + B)(x − 2) + C(x² + 7) kills the first term: 4 − 2 − 13 = C(4 + 7), so −11 = 11C and C = −1. The linear factor's constant is always found first this way.

mcqs.q: In that resolution, comparing the coefficient of x² gives A equal to:
mcqs.why: Comparing x² coefficients: 1 = A + C. With C = −1, this gives A = 2. Then comparing the coefficient of x gives B = 3, completing the unknowns A = 2, B = 3, C = −1.

mcqs.q: (x² − x − 13)/((x² + 7)(x − 2)) resolves into:
mcqs.why: With A = 2, B = 3 and C = −1, the answer is (2x + 3)/(x² + 7) − 1/(x − 2). The minus sign comes from C = −1, and the quadratic factor keeps its linear numerator 2x + 3.

mcqs.q: Resolving (x² − x + 2)/((x + 1)(x² + 3)), putting x = −1 gives A equal to:
mcqs.why: Putting x = −1: 1 + 1 + 2 = A(1 + 3), that is, 4 = 4A, so A = 1. After that, comparing coefficients gives B = 0 and C = −1 for the quadratic factor's numerator Bx + C.

mcqs.q: (x² − x + 2)/((x + 1)(x² + 3)) resolves into:
mcqs.why: With A = 1, B = 0 and C = −1, the quadratic fraction is (0x − 1)/(x² + 3) = −1/(x² + 3). So the full answer is 1/(x + 1) − 1/(x² + 3); since B = 0, only a constant remains over the quadratic factor.

mcqs.q: A quadratic factor like x² + 3 is special because it:
options: Cannot be broken further into factors in real numbers
mcqs.why: Factors such as x² + 7 or x² + 3 cannot be factorised further in real numbers, because x² + 3 = 0 has no real solution. That is exactly why they need the Ax + B numerator treatment.

mcqs.q: The degree of the numerator over a quadratic factor should be:
options: One less than the degree of the denominator factor
mcqs.why: The numerator's degree should be one less than the degree of the denominator factor: a linear factor (degree 1) takes a constant (degree 0), and a quadratic factor (degree 2) takes Ax + B (degree 1). This is the reason stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: In the method of this lesson, after finding C from the linear factor, A and B are found by:
options: Comparing the coefficients of x² and x
Putting the quadratic factor equal to zero in reals
mcqs.why: First put the value which makes the linear factor zero to find C, then find A and B by comparing the coefficients of x² and x. There is no real value making the quadratic factor zero, so comparison is the way for A and B.

lessons.title: Exercise 21.4 — Repeated Quadratic Factors
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Repeated Quadratic Factor?

If an irreducible quadratic factor itself repeats, such as (x² + 1)² or (x² + 3)², a separate fraction is written for each power, and the numerator of each fraction is in the form Ax + B.

P(x) / (x² + 1)² = (Ax + B) / (x² + 1) + (Cx + D) / (x² + 1)²

If a linear factor is also present with it, its own fraction is also written. The unknowns become many, so first one unknown is found by putting the value of the linear factor, and all the rest are found by comparison. Care and order are the success of this lesson.

Example 1: Resolve x² / ((1 + x)(1 + x²)²) into partial fractions

Step 1: Write the form: A / (1 + x) + (Bx + C) / (1 + x²) + (Dx + E) / (1 + x²)².

Step 2: Put x = -1: 1 = A(1 + 1)² = 4A, so A = 1/4.

Step 3: Compare the coefficients: B = -1/4, C = 1/4, D = 1/4, E = 0 are obtained.

Step 4: Write the answer: 1 / (4(1 + x)) + (1 - x) / (4(1 + x²)) + x / (4(1 + x²)²).

Example 2: Resolve 49 / ((x - 2)(3 + x²)²) into partial fractions

Step 1: Write the form: A / (x - 2) + (Bx + C) / (3 + x²) + (Dx + E) / (3 + x²)².

Step 2: Put x = 2: 49 = A(3 + 4)² = 49A, so A = 1.

Step 3: Compare the coefficients: B = -1, C = 1, D = -7, E = -3 are obtained.

Step 4: Write the answer: 1 / (x - 2) + (1 - x) / (3 + x²) + (-7x - 3) / (3 + x²)².

mcqs.q: For a repeated quadratic factor (x² + 1)², the assumed form is:
mcqs.why: If an irreducible quadratic factor itself repeats, a separate fraction is written for each power, and each numerator is in the form Ax + B: (Ax + B)/(x² + 1) + (Cx + D)/(x² + 1)². Both requirements — per power and linear numerators — apply together.

mcqs.q: If a linear factor is also present with a repeated quadratic factor, then:
options: It is merged into the quadratic fractions
Its own fraction is also written
mcqs.why: If a linear factor is also present, its own fraction is also written, as in x²/((1 + x)(1 + x²)²) = A/(1 + x) + (Bx + C)/(1 + x²) + (Dx + E)/(1 + x²)². Every distinct factor contributes its fractions.

mcqs.q: Resolving x²/((1 + x)(1 + x²)²), putting x = −1 gives A equal to:
mcqs.why: Putting x = −1: (−1)² = A(1 + (−1)²)² = A(2)² = 4A, so 1 = 4A and A = 1/4. Comparison then gives B = −1/4, C = 1/4, D = 1/4 and E = 0, as the worked example records.

mcqs.q: x²/((1 + x)(1 + x²)²) resolves into:
options: Only the single fraction x/(4(1 + x²)²)
mcqs.why: With A = 1/4, B = −1/4, C = 1/4, D = 1/4, E = 0, the fractions combine over the common factor 1/4 as 1/(4(1 + x)) + (1 − x)/(4(1 + x²)) + x/(4(1 + x²)²). Note E = 0 removes the constant from the last numerator.

mcqs.q: Resolving 49/((x − 2)(3 + x²)²), putting x = 2 gives A equal to:
mcqs.why: Putting x = 2: 49 = A(3 + 2²)² = A(7)² = 49A, so A = 1. The linear factor's constant is again found first by substitution, before any comparison of coefficients.

mcqs.q: 49/((x − 2)(3 + x²)²) resolves into:
mcqs.why: Comparison gives B = −1, C = 1, D = −7, E = −3 with A = 1. So the answer is 1/(x − 2) + (1 − x)/(3 + x²) + (−7x − 3)/(3 + x²)², with one fraction for the linear factor and one for each power of the quadratic factor.

mcqs.q: In these questions the unknowns are many, so the first one is found by:
options: Putting the value of the linear factor
mcqs.why: The unknowns become many, so first one unknown is found by putting the value of the linear factor (which makes its term survive alone), and all the rest are found by comparison. Care and order are called the success of this lesson.

mcqs.q: Each fraction over a power of a repeated quadratic factor has numerator of the form:
options: A single A for all powers
mcqs.why: The numerator of each fraction is in the form Ax + B — with different letters for each power, such as (Ax + B)/(x² + 1) and (Cx + D)/(x² + 1)². Constants alone would not give enough unknowns to match the identity.

mcqs.q: How many partial fractions does P(x)/(x² + 1)² need (with no other factors)?
mcqs.why: A separate fraction is written for each power: one for (x² + 1)¹ and one for (x² + 1)², so two fractions in total. This mirrors the repeated linear factor rule, but with Ax + B numerators.

mcqs.q: In the first worked example, the value of E (the constant in the last numerator Dx + E) is:
mcqs.why: Comparison of coefficients gives E = 0, which is why the last fraction in the answer is x/(4(1 + x²)²) with no constant term. The other constants are B = −1/4, C = 1/4 and D = 1/4.

lessons.title: Exercise 22.1 — Types of Data and Frequency Tables
lessons.notes_html:
Types of Data

The information collected in statistics is called data. The main types of data are:

Discrete (countable) data: which can be counted, such as the number of people coming to a shopping mall.

Continuous data: which can be measured and can take any value, such as weight, time, age and electricity usage.

Qualitative (categorical) data: which tells a quality, such as colour of eyes, grade, test result (positive or negative) and marital status.

Important Terms of a Frequency Table

Relative frequency = f / N

Percentage frequency = (f / N) x 100

Class mark = (Lower limit + Upper limit) / 2

Range = Maximum value - Minimum value

In cumulative frequency, the frequency of each class goes on being added to all the previous frequencies. To find the real (true) limits, half of the gap between consecutive classes is subtracted from the lower limit and added to the upper limit.

Example 1: Percentage Frequency of Modes of Travel

Out of 20 students: bus: 6, on foot: 7, motorcycle: 2, motor car: 5.

Step 1: Write the total number N = 20.

Step 2: Percentage of bus = (6 / 20) x 100 = 30%.

Step 3: Percentage of on foot = (7 / 20) x 100 = 35%.

Step 4: Percentage of motorcycle = (2 / 20) x 100 = 10%.

Step 5: Percentage of motor car = (5 / 20) x 100 = 25%. The sum of all the percentages is 100%.

Example 2: Continuous Table of Weights — Class Mark and Cumulative Frequency

In the table of weights of 40 students, the range is 57, the classes are 7 and the class width is 9.

Step 1: Mark of the class 119-127 = (119 + 127) / 2 = 123.

Step 2: The real limits of this class are 118.5-127.5 (half the gap 0.5 subtracted and added).

Step 3: The frequency is 3, so the cumulative frequency is also 3.

Step 4: The frequency of the next class 128-136 is 6, so the cumulative frequency = 3 + 6 = 9.

mcqs.q: Data that can be counted, such as the number of people coming to a shopping mall, is called:
mcqs.why: Discrete (countable) data can be counted, like the number of people coming to a shopping mall. Continuous data is measured and can take any value, while qualitative data tells a quality such as eye colour.

mcqs.q: Weight, time, age and electricity usage are examples of:
mcqs.why: These can be measured and can take any value, so they are continuous data. In contrast, counted things are discrete, and qualities like colour of eyes, grade or marital status are qualitative (categorical) data.

mcqs.q: The relative frequency of a class is:
mcqs.why: Relative frequency = f / N, where f is the class frequency and N the total frequency. Multiplying it by 100 gives the percentage frequency: percentage frequency = (f / N) × 100.

mcqs.q: The class mark of a class is:
mcqs.why: Class mark = (Lower limit + Upper limit) / 2, the midpoint of the class. For the class 119–127 in the weights table, the mark is (119 + 127)/2 = 123, as the example computes.

mcqs.q: The range of data is:
mcqs.why: Range = Maximum value − Minimum value. In the weights example the range is 57, with 7 classes of width 9. The range uses only the two extreme values of the data.

mcqs.q: Out of 20 students, 6 travel by bus. The percentage frequency of bus is:
mcqs.why: Percentage frequency = (f / N) × 100 = (6/20) × 100 = 30%. The full table in the example is bus 30%, on foot 35%, motorcycle 10% and motor car 25%, summing to 100%.

mcqs.q: The real (true) limits of a class are found by:
options: Adding the class width to both limits
Subtracting half the gap from the lower limit and adding it to the upper limit
mcqs.why: To find the real limits, half of the gap between consecutive classes is subtracted from the lower limit and added to the upper limit. For 119–127 with gap 1, the real limits are 118.5–127.5.

mcqs.q: In cumulative frequency, each class frequency is:
options: Added to all the previous frequencies
mcqs.why: In cumulative frequency, the frequency of each class goes on being added to all the previous frequencies. In the weights table: 3, then 3 + 6 = 9, then 19, then 30, and so on.

mcqs.q: With frequencies 3 (class 119–127) and 6 (class 128–136), the cumulative frequency up to the second class is:
mcqs.why: Cumulative frequency adds all frequencies up to that class: 3 + 6 = 9. The first class alone has cumulative frequency 3, equal to its own frequency, as the example's table shows.

mcqs.q: Colour of eyes, grade and marital status are examples of:
mcqs.why: These tell a quality rather than a number, so they are qualitative (categorical) data. The notes also list test result (positive or negative) as qualitative, while counts are discrete and measurements are continuous.

lessons.title: Exercise 22.2 — Histogram, Frequency Polygon and Ogive
lessons.notes_html:
Histogram

In a histogram, continuous rectangles are drawn on the real limits. There are classes on the x-axis and frequencies on the y-axis. There is no gap between the rectangles, because the classes are continuous by real limits.

Frequency Polygon

The midpoints of the top sides of each rectangle are marked, all the points are joined by straight lines, and the line is brought down to the x-axis on both sides. The other method: join the points of frequencies at the class marks.

Cumulative Frequency Curve — Ogive

For an ogive, at the upper real limit of each class its cumulative frequency is marked. The start is from zero at the lower real limit, and the points are joined by a smooth curve. The median and quartiles can also be found from an ogive.

Adjustment for Unequal Class Widths

If the widths of the classes are not equal, the height of the rectangle is adjusted so that the area remains in proportion to the frequency.

Adjusted height = Frequency x (Smallest width / Class width)

Example: Marks 1 to 5, frequencies 2, 5, 4, 3, 1

Step 1: Write the total number N = 2 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 15.

Step 2: Find the percentage frequencies: 13.33%, 33.33%, 26.67%, 20%, 6.67%.

Step 3: Find the cumulative frequencies: 2, 7, 11, 14, 15.

Step 4: For the histogram, draw at each mark a rectangle of the height of its frequency.

Step 5: For the polygon, join the midpoints of the tops of the rectangles and bring it down to the x-axis on both sides.

Step 6: For the ogive, join the points (0.5, 0), (1.5, 2), (2.5, 7), (3.5, 11), (4.5, 14), (5.5, 15).

Example 2: Unequal Widths — Adjusted Height

The classes are 0-39, 40-49, 50-79, 80-99 and the frequencies 6, 8, 12, 4. The smallest width d = 10.

Step 1: Write the real limits: -0.5-39.5, 39.5-49.5, 49.5-79.5, 79.5-99.5.

Step 2: The width of the first class is 40: height = 6 x (10/40) = 1.5.

Step 3: The width of the second class is 10: height = 8 x (10/10) = 8.

Step 4: The width of the third class is 30: height = 12 x (10/30) = 4.

Step 5: The width of the fourth class is 20: height = 4 x (10/20) = 2. Draw the rectangles with these heights.

mcqs.q: In a histogram, the rectangles are drawn:
options: With gaps between them, on the class marks
Continuously on the real limits, with no gap
mcqs.why: In a histogram, continuous rectangles are drawn on the real limits, classes on the x-axis and frequencies on the y-axis. There is no gap between the rectangles, because the classes are continuous by real limits.

mcqs.q: A frequency polygon is drawn by:
options: Joining the corners of the rectangles
Marking the midpoints of the top sides of the rectangles and joining them, bringing the line down to the x-axis on both sides
Drawing a smooth curve through the upper limits
mcqs.why: The midpoints of the top sides of each rectangle are marked, all the points are joined by straight lines, and the line is brought down to the x-axis on both sides. The other method joins the frequency points at the class marks.

mcqs.q: For an ogive, at each class we plot:
options: The frequency at the lower real limit
The cumulative frequency at the upper real limit
mcqs.why: For an ogive, at the upper real limit of each class its cumulative frequency is marked, starting from zero at the lower real limit, and the points are joined by a smooth curve. The median and quartiles can also be found from an ogive.

mcqs.q: For marks 1 to 5 with frequencies 2, 5, 4, 3, 1, the total N is:
mcqs.why: N = 2 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 15. From this the percentage frequencies 13.33%, 33.33%, 26.67%, 20% and 6.67% and the cumulative frequencies 2, 7, 11, 14, 15 are computed in the example.

mcqs.q: The cumulative frequencies for that data are:
mcqs.why: Keep adding: 2; 2 + 5 = 7; 7 + 4 = 11; 11 + 3 = 14; 14 + 1 = 15. The last cumulative frequency equals N = 15, which checks the arithmetic, and these values feed the ogive points.

mcqs.q: When class widths are unequal, the adjusted height of a histogram rectangle is:
mcqs.why: Adjusted height = Frequency × (Smallest width / Class width), so that the area stays in proportion to the frequency. For the width-40 class with frequency 6 and smallest width 10, the height is 6 × 10/40 = 1.5.

mcqs.q: Classes 0–39, 40–49, 50–79, 80–99 have frequencies 6, 8, 12, 4 and smallest width 10. The adjusted height for the class 50–79 (width 30) is:
mcqs.why: Height = 12 × (10/30) = 4. The other heights are 1.5 (width 40), 8 (width 10) and 2 (width 20); adjusting ensures a wide class does not look more frequent than it is.

mcqs.q: The ogive for the marks example starts from the point:
mcqs.why: The ogive joins the points (0.5, 0), (1.5, 2), (2.5, 7), (3.5, 11), (4.5, 14), (5.5, 15): it starts from zero at the lower real limit of the first class and rises by the cumulative frequencies at each upper real limit.

mcqs.q: From an ogive we can also find:
mcqs.why: The notes state that the median and quartiles can also be found from an ogive, by reading across from the cumulative levels. The ogive is the cumulative frequency curve, drawn as a smooth curve.

mcqs.q: The frequency polygon can also be drawn by joining:
options: The points of frequencies at the class marks
The cumulative points with a curve
mcqs.why: The other method for a frequency polygon is to join the points of frequencies plotted at the class marks. Both methods give the same polygon shape; the class-mark method does not even need the histogram first.

lessons.title: Exercise 22.3 — Measures of Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode
lessons.notes_html:
What are the Measures of Central Tendency?

These measures tell what the central or representative value of the data is. The main measures are five: arithmetic mean (A.M.), geometric mean (G.M.), harmonic mean (H.M.), median and mode.

Mean = Sum of values / Number of values

Grouped Mean = Σfx / Σf

G.M. = n-th root of (x1 x x2 x ... x xn)

H.M. = n / Σ(1 / x)

For the median, the data is arranged in order and the middle observation is found. The mode is the observation which comes most often. G.M. and H.M. are found only when all the numbers are positive; if there is a negative number or zero, they are not possible. For qualitative data, A.M., G.M. and H.M. are not possible.

Important Properties

Σ(x - Mean) = 0

For Y = aX + b: New Mean = a x Mean of X + b

Step-deviation method: Mean = A + h x (Σfu / Σf)

Example: Data 51, 55, 52, 54, 58, 60, 61, 62, 52, 57, 52, 64

Step 1: Write the total number n = 12.

Step 2: Find the sum of all the numbers: Σx = 678.

Step 3: A.M. = 678 / 12 = 56.5.

Step 4: Arrange in order: 51, 52, 52, 52, 54, 55, 57, 58, 60, 61, 62, 64. The two middle numbers are 55 and 57, so the median = (55 + 57) / 2 = 56.

Step 5: The most repeated number is 52 (3 times), so the mode = 52.

Step 6: G.M. ≈ 56.33 and H.M. ≈ 56.18. Note: 56.5 > 56.33 > 56.18, that is, A.M. > G.M. > H.M.

Example 2: What happens if there is a negative number?

For the data 3.2, 6, 10, 12, 12, -20, 25, 28, 30.8:

Step 1: Sum = 107 and n = 9, so A.M. = 107 / 9 ≈ 11.89.

Step 2: One number -20 is negative, so G.M. and H.M. are not possible.

Step 3: In order, the middle (5th) number is 12, so the median = 12, and the mode is also 12 (it came twice).

mcqs.q: The arithmetic mean of data is:
options: Number of values / sum of values
Sum of values × number of values
Sum of values / number of values
mcqs.why: Mean = Sum of values / Number of values. For the example data with Σx = 678 and n = 12, the mean is 678/12 = 56.5. For grouped data the corresponding formula is Σfx / Σf.

mcqs.q: The geometric mean of n values is:
options: The n-th root of the product x1 × x2 × ... × xn
mcqs.why: G.M. = n-th root of (x1 × x2 × ... × xn). The harmonic mean is instead H.M. = n / Σ(1/x). Both need all values positive, as the notes insist.
The mode is the observation which comes most often. The value 52 appears 3 times, more than any other, so the mode is 52. In the same example the mean is 56.5 and the median is 56.

mcqs.q: For that same data, the median is:
mcqs.why: Arranged in order, the two middle numbers (6th and 7th of 12) are 55 and 57, so the median = (55 + 57)/2 = 56. The median uses the ordered positions, unlike the mean 56.5 which uses every value.

mcqs.q: The relation seen in the example between the three means is:
mcqs.why: The example gives A.M. = 56.5, G.M. ≈ 56.33 and H.M. ≈ 56.18, so 56.5 > 56.33 > 56.18, that is, A.M. > G.M. > H.M. The same order holds in the weighted example of the next lesson.

mcqs.q: A key property of the arithmetic mean is that:
mcqs.why: The sum of the deviations of the values from their arithmetic mean is always zero: Σ(x − Mean) = 0. The positive and negative deviations exactly cancel, which is a defining balance property of the mean.

mcqs.q: If Y = aX + b, then the mean of Y is:
mcqs.why: For Y = aX + b: New Mean = a × Mean of X + b. In the later example, the mean of Z = 3W − 11 is 3 × 156.375 − 11 = 458.125, applying exactly this rule.

mcqs.q: G.M. and H.M. are not possible when the data contains:
mcqs.why: G.M. and H.M. are found only when all the numbers are positive; if there is a negative number or zero, they are not possible. The example data containing −20 still has A.M. ≈ 11.89, median 12 and mode 12.

mcqs.q: In the step-deviation method, the mean is:
mcqs.why: Step-deviation method: Mean = A + h × (Σfu / Σf), where A is the assumed mean and h the class width. It is a shortcut form of the grouped mean Σfx / Σf given in the same lesson.

mcqs.q: For qualitative data, which measures are not possible?
mcqs.why: For qualitative data, A.M., G.M. and H.M. are not possible, because qualities cannot be added, multiplied or reciprocated meaningfully. Categorical data can still be summarised by counts and percentages, as in the earlier lesson.

lessons.title: Exercise 22.4 — Weighted Mean, Moving Average and Measures from Graphs
lessons.notes_html:
Weighted Mean

When the importance of each observation is different, each value is multiplied by its weight (w) and the weighted mean is found.

Weighted Mean = Σwx / Σw

The combined mean of two groups is also found by the same formula — the number of items of each group is its weight.

Moving Average

To see the trend in data changing with time, the mean of a few consecutive values is taken out, and then, moving one step forward, another mean is taken out. In a 3-day moving average, 3 consecutive days are added each time and divided by 3. To bring a mean of an even period (such as 4 days) to the centre, the mean of two consecutive means is taken again; it is called the centred moving average.

Measures from Graphs

The median and quartiles are found from an ogive: from the point of N/2, N/4 and 3N/4 a horizontal line is drawn to the ogive and then down to the x-axis. The mode is found from a histogram.

Example 1: Combined Mean of 50 Bags of Fruit

The mean weight of 21 bags is 24.2 kg and of 29 bags is 23.6 kg.

Step 1: First group: 21 x 24.2 = 508.2.

Step 2: Second group: 29 x 23.6 = 684.4.

Step 3: Total sum = 508.2 + 684.4 = 1192.6.

Step 4: Weighted mean = 1192.6 / 50 = 23.852 kg.

Example 2: Sum of the Deviations of W from its A.M.

W = {148, 145, 160, 157, 156, 160, 160, 165}.

Step 1: Sum ΣW = 1251 and n = 8.

Step 2: A.M. = 1251 / 8 = 156.375.

Step 3: Σ(W - Mean) = ΣW - 8 x 156.375 = 1251 - 1251 = 0.

Step 4: It is proved that the sum of the deviations from the A.M. is always zero. For the same W, the A.M. of Z = 3W - 11 is 3 x 156.375 - 11 = 458.125.

Example 3: Weighted Mean of Prices of Household Items

Step 1: Σw = 45 and Σwx = 14850 are given.

Step 2: Weighted A.M. = 14850 / 45 = 330.

Step 3: Weighted G.M. ≈ 310.8 and weighted H.M. = 45 / 0.151615 ≈ 296.80.

Step 4: Here also the order A.M. > G.M. > H.M. holds.

mcqs.q: The weighted mean is:
mcqs.why: Weighted Mean = Σwx / Σw: each value is multiplied by its weight w, the products are added, and the sum is divided by the total of the weights. It is used when the importance of each observation is different.

mcqs.q: The combined mean of two groups is found by the same weighted-mean formula, where each group's weight is:
mcqs.why: The combined mean of two groups is also found by the weighted formula — the number of items of each group is its weight. So the group totals (items × mean) are added and divided by the total number of items.

mcqs.q: A moving average is used to:
options: See the trend in data changing with time
mcqs.why: To see the trend in data changing with time, the mean of a few consecutive values is taken, and then, moving one step forward, another mean is taken. In a 3-day moving average, 3 consecutive days are added each time and divided by 3.

mcqs.q: For an even period such as 4 days, the centred moving average is obtained by:
options: Taking the mean of two consecutive moving averages again
mcqs.why: To bring a mean of an even period (such as 4 days) to the centre, the mean of two consecutive means is taken again; it is called the centred moving average. This aligns the average with the middle of its period.

mcqs.q: From an ogive, the median and quartiles are read at the levels:
mcqs.why: The median and quartiles are found from an ogive: from the point of N/2, N/4 and 3N/4 a horizontal line is drawn to the ogive and then down to the x-axis. The mode, in contrast, is found from a histogram.

mcqs.q: The mean weight of 21 bags is 24.2 kg and of 29 bags is 23.6 kg. The combined mean of all 50 bags is:
mcqs.why: Group totals: 21 × 24.2 = 508.2 and 29 × 23.6 = 684.4, giving a total sum of 1192.6 over 50 bags. Weighted mean = 1192.6/50 = 23.852 kg, lying closer to the larger group's mean, as it should.
ΣW = 1251 and n = 8, so A.M. = 1251/8 = 156.375. This mean is then used to show Σ(W − Mean) = 1251 − 8 × 156.375 = 0, confirming the zero-deviation property.

mcqs.q: If the mean of W is 156.375, the mean of Z = 3W − 11 is:
mcqs.why: Using the rule for Y = aX + b: mean of Z = 3 × 156.375 − 11 = 469.125 − 11 = 458.125. Both the multiplication by 3 and the subtraction of 11 carry over to the mean exactly.

mcqs.q: Given Σw = 45 and Σwx = 14850 for prices of household items, the weighted A.M. is:
mcqs.why: Weighted A.M. = Σwx / Σw = 14850/45 = 330. In the same example the weighted G.M. is about 310.8 and the weighted H.M. about 296.80, so the order A.M. > G.M. > H.M. holds here too.

mcqs.q: In a 3-day moving average, each value is:
options: The mean of 3 consecutive days, then moved one step forward
The mean of all days so far
mcqs.why: In a 3-day moving average, 3 consecutive days are added each time and divided by 3; then the window moves one step forward and the mean is taken again. Repeating this traces the trend of the time data.

lessons.title: Exercise 22.5 — Measures of Dispersion: Range, Variance and Standard Deviation
lessons.notes_html:
What are the Measures of Dispersion?

A central measure tells only the centre, but how much the data is spread is told by the measures of dispersion: range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation. The data whose standard deviation is smaller is more uniform and consistent.

Range = Maximum - Minimum

Variance = Σ(x - Mean)² / n

Standard Deviation = Square root of Variance

Mean Deviation = Σ|x - Mean| / n

To find a relative measure, the absolute measure is divided by the mean, such as relative standard deviation = S.D. / Mean. The range is based on only two extreme values, so it can also be misleading.

Example: Number of Absent Students 3, 5, 3, 2, 4, 1, 8

Step 1: Range = 8 - 1 = 7.

Step 2: Sum = 26 and n = 7, so A.M. = 26 / 7 ≈ 3.714.

Step 3: Take the deviation of each value from the A.M., square them and add: Variance = 1540 / 343 ≈ 4.49.

Step 4: Standard deviation = √4.49 ≈ 2.12.

Step 5: Mean deviation = 82 / 49 ≈ 1.67.

Example 2: Which Player is More Consistent?

Step 1: The standard deviation of player A is ≈ 66.54 and the range 185.

Step 2: The standard deviation of player B is ≈ 24.53 and the range 72.

Step 3: The standard deviation of B is smaller, so B performs with more consistency.

Remember: In a distribution of 50 pieces of metal, the range is 2.10, the variance ≈ 0.196 and the standard deviation ≈ 0.443 — the variance is always the square of the standard deviation.

mcqs.q: The measures of dispersion tell us:
options: How much the data is spread
mcqs.why: A central measure tells only the centre, but how much the data is spread is told by the measures of dispersion: range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation. The two families answer different questions about data.

mcqs.q: The variance is:
mcqs.why: Variance = Σ(x − Mean)² / n: deviations from the mean are squared, added and divided by n. The standard deviation is then the square root of the variance, restoring the original units.

mcqs.q: The standard deviation is:
options: The square root of the variance
mcqs.why: Standard Deviation = Square root of Variance, so variance is always the square of the standard deviation. In the metal-pieces example, variance ≈ 0.196 and S.D. ≈ 0.443, and indeed 0.443² ≈ 0.196.

mcqs.q: The mean deviation is:
mcqs.why: Mean Deviation = Σ|x − Mean| / n: the absolute deviations are averaged, without squaring. For the absent-students data it is 82/49 ≈ 1.67, smaller than the standard deviation 2.12 because squaring is not used.

mcqs.q: Data whose standard deviation is smaller is:
mcqs.why: The data whose standard deviation is smaller is more uniform and consistent. This is why player B, with the smaller standard deviation, is judged the more consistent performer in the example.

mcqs.q: A relative measure such as relative standard deviation is obtained by:
options: Dividing the absolute measure by the mean
mcqs.why: To find a relative measure, the absolute measure is divided by the mean, such as relative standard deviation = S.D. / Mean. Relative measures allow spread to be compared between data sets with different sizes or units.

mcqs.q: For the absent students 3, 5, 3, 2, 4, 1, 8, the range is:
mcqs.why: Range = Maximum − Minimum = 8 − 1 = 7. The range is based on only the two extreme values, so it can be misleading, as the notes caution, even though it is the quickest measure of spread.

mcqs.q: For the same data, the variance is approximately:
mcqs.why: The mean is 26/7 ≈ 3.714; squaring and adding the deviations gives Variance = 1540/343 ≈ 4.49. Then the standard deviation is √4.49 ≈ 2.12, and the mean deviation is about 1.67 — three different measures, not to be confused.

mcqs.q: Player A has S.D. ≈ 66.54 and player B has S.D. ≈ 24.53. Who is more consistent?
mcqs.why: The standard deviation of B is smaller (24.53 against 66.54), and B's range is also smaller (72 against 185). Smaller spread means B performs with more consistency, as the example concludes.

mcqs.q: The range can be misleading because it is based on:
mcqs.why: The range is based on only two extreme values, the maximum and the minimum, so a single unusual value can distort it. Variance and standard deviation are safer because they use every observation's deviation from the mean.

lessons.title: Pythagoras Theorem — Proof and Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Pythagoras Theorem — Statement

In a right-angled triangle, the biggest side is the hypotenuse, which is opposite the right angle (90°). The other two sides are the legs. The theorem says:

c² = a² + b²

That is, the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides. If a or b is to be found:

a² = c² - b² , b² = c² - a²

Outline of the Proof — Step by Step

Step 1: Take a right-angled triangle ABC in which the right angle is at C and the hypotenuse AB = c.

Step 2: Construct a square on the hypotenuse and squares on the other two sides also.

Step 3: Divide the area of the big square into smaller squares and triangles and calculate.

Step 4: The calculation shows that the area of the square on the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the areas of the other two squares.

Step 5: So c² = a² + b² is proved.

Converse

If in a triangle the square of one side is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides, then that triangle is right-angled, and the angle opposite the biggest side is 90°. For example, for 16, 30, 34: 16² + 30² = 256 + 900 = 1156 = 34², so the triangle is right-angled.

Example 1: Sides 7 and 24; find the hypotenuse

Step 1: Write the formula: x² = 7² + 24².

Step 2: Find the squares: 7² = 49 and 24² = 576.

Step 3: Add: x² = 49 + 576 = 625.

Step 4: Take the square root: x = 25.

Example 2: Hypotenuse 13 and one side 5; find the other side

Step 1: Write the formula: x² = 13² - 5².

Step 2: Find the squares: 169 - 25 = 144.

Step 3: Take the square root: x = 12.

Example 3: The Ladder Question

The foot of a ladder is 6 ft away from a wall and its top is 8 ft high on the wall.

Step 1: The wall, the ground and the ladder form a right-angled triangle; the ladder is the hypotenuse.

Step 2: Length² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100.

Step 3: Length = √100 = 10 ft.

Other Applications

Diagonal of a rectangle: if the sides are 50 m and 30 m, the diagonal = √(50² + 30²) = √3400 = 10√34 ≈ 58.31 m. The altitude of an equilateral triangle (side 8) = √(8² - 4²) = √48 = 4√3 ≈ 6.93 units. In an isosceles triangle (sides 12, 12 and base 10), the altitude divides the base into 5 and 5, and the altitude = √(12² - 5²) = √119 ≈ 10.91 cm.

mcqs.q: Pythagoras' theorem states that in a right-angled triangle:
mcqs.why: The square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides: c² = a² + b². The hypotenuse is the biggest side, opposite the right angle (90°), and the other two sides are the legs.

mcqs.q: If the hypotenuse c and one leg b are known, the other leg a is found by:
mcqs.why: Rearranging c² = a² + b² gives a² = c² − b² (and likewise b² = c² − a²). For hypotenuse 13 and side 5 this gives a² = 169 − 25 = 144, so a = 12, as in the second example.

mcqs.q: The converse of Pythagoras' theorem says: if the square of one side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, then the triangle is:
options: Right-angled, with the right angle opposite the biggest side
mcqs.why: If in a triangle the square of one side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle is right-angled, and the angle opposite the biggest side is 90°. For 16, 30, 34: 256 + 900 = 1156 = 34², so it is right-angled.

mcqs.q: For sides 7 and 24, the hypotenuse is:
mcqs.why: x² = 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625, so x = √625 = 25. The triple 7-24-25 is one of the standard right-triangle triples met in this chapter.

mcqs.q: A ladder's foot is 6 ft from a wall and its top reaches 8 ft high on the wall. The ladder's length is:
mcqs.why: The wall, ground and ladder form a right-angled triangle with the ladder as hypotenuse: Length² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100, so the length is √100 = 10 ft.

mcqs.q: The diagonal of a rectangle with sides 50 m and 30 m is:
mcqs.why: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of the right triangle with legs 50 and 30: √(50² + 30²) = √(2500 + 900) = √3400 = 10√34 ≈ 58.31 m, as computed under 'Other Applications' in the notes.

mcqs.q: The altitude of an equilateral triangle of side 8 is:
mcqs.why: The altitude bisects the base, giving a right triangle with hypotenuse 8 and one leg 4: altitude = √(8² − 4²) = √48 = 4√3 ≈ 6.93 units. Halving the base first is the key step.

mcqs.q: In an isosceles triangle with sides 12, 12 and base 10, the altitude is:
mcqs.why: The altitude divides the base into 5 and 5, so altitude = √(12² − 5²) = √(144 − 25) = √119 ≈ 10.91 cm. The equal side 12 is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the altitude.

mcqs.q: In the proof outline, the squares are constructed on:
options: The hypotenuse and on the other two sides also
mcqs.why: Step 2 of the proof outline: construct a square on the hypotenuse and squares on the other two sides also. Dividing and calculating the areas then shows the hypotenuse square equals the sum of the other two squares, proving c² = a² + b².

mcqs.q: The hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle is the side:
mcqs.why: In a right-angled triangle, the biggest side is the hypotenuse, which is opposite the right angle (90°). The other two sides meeting at the right angle are called the legs, and their squares add to the hypotenuse's square.

lessons.title: Exercise 24.1 — Basic Proportionality Theorem and Its Converse
lessons.notes_html:
Basic Proportionality Theorem

If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle, it divides the other two sides in the same ratio. In ΔABC, if DE ∥ BC, then:

AD / DB = AE / EC

Outline of the proof: Divide AD and AE into equal units. Due to the parallel lines, the corresponding parts become equal, so the ratio of the parts remains the same on both sides.

Converse

If a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side. That is, if AD / DB = AE / EC, then DE ∥ BC.

Midpoint Result

A line drawn from the midpoint of one side of a triangle parallel to another side bisects the third side. Because at the midpoint AD = DB, so the ratio becomes 1 and AE = EC is obtained.

Example 1: Find mCE — mDC = 12 cm, mBD = 6 cm, mAE = 5 cm, DE ∥ AB

Step 1: Write the theorem: mCE / mAE = mDC / mBD.

Step 2: Put the values: mCE / 5 = 12 / 6.

Step 3: 12 / 6 = 2, so mCE = 5 x 2 = 10 cm.

Example 2: Find x — mAP = 5x - 3, mPB = 2, mAQ = 2x + 1, mQC = 3, PQ ∥ BC

Step 1: Write the theorem: (5x - 3) / 2 = (2x + 1) / 3.

Step 2: Cross-multiply: 3(5x - 3) = 2(2x + 1), that is, 15x - 9 = 4x + 2.

Step 3: Bring the x terms to one side: 15x - 4x = 2 + 9, that is, 11x = 11.

Step 4: x = 1.

mcqs.q: The Basic Proportionality Theorem says: if a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle, it divides the other two sides:
options: In the ratio of the angles
mcqs.why: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle, it divides the other two sides in the same ratio: in ΔABC with DE ∥ BC, AD/DB = AE/EC. This equal-ratio conclusion is the heart of the theorem.

mcqs.q: The converse states: if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is:
options: A bisector of the third side
mcqs.why: The converse: if AD/DB = AE/EC, then DE ∥ BC. Equal ratios on the two sides force the line to be parallel to the third side, reversing the direction of the Basic Proportionality Theorem.

mcqs.q: A line drawn from the midpoint of one side of a triangle parallel to another side:
options: Is perpendicular to the third side
mcqs.why: At the midpoint AD = DB, so the ratio AD/DB becomes 1, and the theorem gives AE = EC: the line bisects the third side. This midpoint result is a direct special case of the theorem.

mcqs.q: In the proof outline of the theorem, AD and AE are:
options: Divided into equal units, and the parallel lines make the corresponding parts equal
mcqs.why: Divide AD and AE into equal units; due to the parallel lines, the corresponding parts become equal, so the ratio of the parts remains the same on both sides. This equal-parts idea is the outline of the proof in the notes.

mcqs.q: With DE ∥ AB, mDC = 12 cm, mBD = 6 cm and mAE = 5 cm, mCE equals:
mcqs.why: By the theorem, mCE/mAE = mDC/mBD, so mCE/5 = 12/6 = 2, giving mCE = 5 × 2 = 10 cm. The ratio on one side of the triangle equals the ratio on the other side.

mcqs.q: In that example the theorem is applied in the form:
mcqs.why: Step 1 of the example writes the theorem as mCE/mAE = mDC/mBD: the parts on one side are in the same ratio as the parts on the other side. Substituting the numbers then gives mCE = 10 cm.

mcqs.q: With mAP = 5x − 3, mPB = 2, mAQ = 2x + 1, mQC = 3 and PQ ∥ BC, the equation is:
mcqs.why: The theorem gives AP/PB = AQ/QC, so (5x − 3)/2 = (2x + 1)/3. Cross-multiplying: 3(5x − 3) = 2(2x + 1), that is, 15x − 9 = 4x + 2, from which x is found.

mcqs.q: Solving that equation gives x equal to:
mcqs.why: 15x − 9 = 4x + 2 gives 15x − 4x = 2 + 9, so 11x = 11 and x = 1. Checking with x = 1: AP = 2, PB = 2, AQ = 3, QC = 3, and the ratios are equal as required.

mcqs.q: At the midpoint of a side, the ratio AD/DB becomes:
mcqs.why: At the midpoint AD = DB, so AD/DB = 1. The theorem then forces AE/EC = 1 as well, i.e. AE = EC, which is why the parallel line through a midpoint bisects the opposite side.

mcqs.q: In Example 1, since mDC/mBD = 12/6 = 2, mCE must be:
mcqs.why: mCE/mAE = mDC/mBD = 2, so mCE = 2 × mAE = 2 × 5 = 10 cm. Whatever ratio the parts of one side make, the parts of the other side make the same ratio — the content of the theorem.

lessons.title: Exercise 24.2 — Angle Bisector Theorem and Similar Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
Angle Bisector Theorem

The bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the opposite side in the ratio of the other two sides. In ΔABC, if AD is the bisector of ∠A, then:

BD / DC = AB / AC

Similar Triangles

Two triangles whose angles are equal and whose corresponding sides are proportional are similar. The symbol is ~, such as ΔABC ~ ΔPQR. All equilateral triangles are always similar. By the AA rule: if two angles are equal, the triangles are similar.

Ratio of areas = (Ratio of corresponding sides)²

In a right triangle, the perpendicular drawn from the right angle to the hypotenuse makes two smaller triangles, and each of them is similar to the original triangle (by AA, due to the common angle and the 90° angle).

Example 1: x with the bisector — mAB = x + 9, mAC = 11 - x, mCD = 2x + 3, mBD = 3x + 2

Step 1: Write the theorem: (x + 9) / (11 - x) = (3x + 2) / (2x + 3).

Step 2: Cross-multiply and solve: 5x² - 10x + 5 = 0 is obtained.

Step 3: Divide by 5: x² - 2x + 1 = 0, that is, (x - 1)² = 0.

Step 4: x = 1.

Example 2: Area of similar triangles — A1 = 28 cm², mAB = 4x cm, mPQ = 2x cm

Step 1: Write the formula: A1 / A2 = (mAB / mPQ)².

Step 2: Put the values: (4x / 2x)² = 2² = 4.

Step 3: 28 / A2 = 4, so A2 = 28 / 4 = 7 cm².

Example 3: x from the ratio of sides — ratio x - 5 : 2 and ratio of areas 1 : 9

Step 1: Write ((x - 5) / 2)² = 1 / 9.

Step 2: Take the square root: (x - 5) / 2 = 1 / 3 (length is positive).

Step 3: x - 5 = 2 / 3, so x = 17 / 3.

mcqs.q: The Angle Bisector Theorem states that the bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the opposite side in the ratio of:
mcqs.why: In ΔABC, if AD is the bisector of ∠A, then BD/DC = AB/AC: the opposite side is divided in the ratio of the other two sides (the sides forming the bisected angle). This is the Angle Bisector Theorem.

mcqs.q: Two triangles are similar when:
options: Their angles are equal and corresponding sides are proportional
mcqs.why: Two triangles whose angles are equal and whose corresponding sides are proportional are similar, denoted by ~, such as ΔABC ~ ΔPQR. Equal angles alone (by AA) force the sides to be proportional.

mcqs.q: Which statement about equilateral triangles is true?
options: All equilateral triangles are always similar
They are similar only to right triangles
They are similar only if equal in size
mcqs.why: All equilateral triangles are always similar, because every angle is 60° in each, so the AA condition is satisfied whatever the sizes. Their sides are then automatically in proportion.

mcqs.q: By the AA rule, two triangles are similar if:
options: Two angles of one are equal to two angles of the other
One angle and one side are equal
mcqs.why: By the AA rule: if two angles are equal, the triangles are similar — the third angles then match as well, since the angles of a triangle sum to 180°. This is the rule used for the right-triangle result in the notes.

mcqs.q: For similar triangles, the ratio of their areas equals:
options: The cube of the ratio of sides
The square of the ratio of corresponding sides
mcqs.why: Ratio of areas = (Ratio of corresponding sides)². So if corresponding sides are in ratio 2 : 1, the areas are in ratio 4 : 1, a fact used in both worked examples of this lesson.

mcqs.q: In a right triangle, the perpendicular from the right angle to the hypotenuse creates two smaller triangles that are:
options: Each similar to the original triangle
mcqs.why: Each smaller triangle is similar to the original triangle (by AA, due to the common angle and the 90° angle). The perpendicular to the hypotenuse thus splits the right triangle into two triangles of the same shape as itself.

mcqs.q: With mAB = x + 9, mAC = 11 − x, mCD = 2x + 3, mBD = 3x + 2, the bisector theorem leads to x equal to:
mcqs.why: Writing (x + 9)/(11 − x) = (3x + 2)/(2x + 3) and cross-multiplying gives 5x² − 10x + 5 = 0. Dividing by 5: x² − 2x + 1 = (x − 1)² = 0, so x = 1, as the example solves.

mcqs.q: Similar triangles have A1 = 28 cm², with corresponding sides mAB = 4x cm and mPQ = 2x cm. The other area A2 is:
mcqs.why: A1/A2 = (mAB/mPQ)² = (4x/2x)² = 2² = 4. So 28/A2 = 4, giving A2 = 28/4 = 7 cm². The side ratio is only 2, but areas scale with the square of the ratio.

mcqs.q: If the ratio of corresponding sides is (x − 5) : 2 and the ratio of areas is 1 : 9, then x equals:
mcqs.why: ((x − 5)/2)² = 1/9. Taking the square root (lengths are positive): (x − 5)/2 = 1/3, so x − 5 = 2/3 and x = 5 + 2/3 = 17/3, exactly as the third example finds.

mcqs.q: If two similar triangles have corresponding sides in ratio 2 : 1, their areas are in ratio:
mcqs.why: Areas go as the square of the side ratio: 2² : 1² = 4 : 1. This is exactly the step (4x/2x)² = 4 used to get A2 = 7 cm² from A1 = 28 cm² in the worked example.

lessons.title: Exercise 25.1 — Circle through Three Points and Circumcentre
lessons.notes_html:
Circle and Points — Basic Facts

A circle is a closed and simple curved line. Every point of a circle is at the same distance from the centre. This distance is called the radius.

A chord is a line segment joining two points of a circle. The diameter is the chord which passes through the centre, and the diameter is twice the radius.

Three Collinear Points

Three points which lie on the same straight line are called collinear points.

Result: No circle can pass through three collinear points.

Reason: The perpendicular bisectors of collinear points are parallel to each other and never meet, so no centre is obtained.

Theorem — One and Only One Circle through Three Non-Collinear Points

Statement: One and only one circle can pass through three non-collinear points.

The hypothesis of this statement is: three points are non-collinear.

The conclusion of this statement is: one and only one circle passes through the three points.

Proof — Circle through the Vertices of a Triangle (Step by Step)

Step 1: Take the three sides of the triangle and draw the perpendicular bisector of each side.

Step 2: The perpendicular bisectors of the three sides meet at one and the same point O.

Step 3: The point O is at the same distance from all three vertices, that is, OA = OB = OC.

Step 4: So the circle with centre O and radius OA passes through all three vertices.

Step 5: The meeting point O is only one, so this circle is the only circle.

Remember: The point O is called the circumcentre of the triangle.

Four Points and a Cyclic Quadrilateral

It is not necessary that a circle passes through every four non-collinear points.

A circle will pass through four points only when they are concyclic.

In general, the circle of three points does not pass through the fourth point.

For a cyclic quadrilateral, the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at one and the same point O, and O is at the same distance from all four vertices, so the circle with centre O passes through all four vertices, and it is the only circle.

Worked Example — A Mosque at Equal Distance from Three Villages

Question: Village B is 6 km to the east of village A, and village C is 8 km to the north of village B. Where should the mosque be so that it is at an equal distance from every village?

Step 1: In the figure, O is the centre of the circle and AB is a chord — here the triangle ABC is formed, and the mosque is its circumcentre.

Step 2: AC = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 km.

Step 3: ∠B = 90°, so the circumcentre is the midpoint of AC.

Step 4: Distance from every village = 10/2 = 5 km.

Answer: The mosque should be at the midpoint of AC, and every villager will have to travel 5 km.

Things to Remember

All circles are always similar. Circles of equal measure are both congruent and similar.

mcqs.q: Three points which lie on the same straight line are called:
mcqs.why: Three points which lie on the same straight line are called collinear points. The lesson's key result is that no circle can pass through three collinear points, because their perpendicular bisectors are parallel and never meet.

mcqs.q: How many circles can pass through three non-collinear points?
mcqs.why: One and only one circle can pass through three non-collinear points. The perpendicular bisectors of the three sides meet at a single point O with OA = OB = OC, and that unique meeting point gives the unique circle.

mcqs.q: In the theorem on the circle through three points, the hypothesis is:
options: The points form a right triangle
mcqs.why: The hypothesis of the statement is that the three points are non-collinear; the conclusion is that one and only one circle passes through the three points. Keeping hypothesis and conclusion apart is part of understanding any theorem.

mcqs.q: The point where the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle's sides meet is called the:
mcqs.why: The meeting point O of the perpendicular bisectors is the circumcentre of the triangle. It is at the same distance from all three vertices, so the circle centred at O with radius OA passes through A, B and C.

mcqs.q: Why can no circle pass through three collinear points?
options: The points are too close together
A circle is a curved line
Their perpendicular bisectors are parallel and never meet, so no centre is obtained
mcqs.why: The perpendicular bisectors of collinear points are parallel to each other and never meet, so no centre is obtained. Without a centre, no circle through all three points can be drawn — the reason given in the notes.

mcqs.q: In the mosque example, villages A, B, C form a right triangle with AC = 10 km and ∠B = 90°. The mosque (equidistant from all villages) should be at:
mcqs.why: Since ∠B = 90°, the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse AC. With AC = √(6² + 8²) = 10 km, the distance from the midpoint to every village is 10/2 = 5 km, so the mosque goes at the midpoint of AC.

mcqs.q: In the mosque example, AC equals:
mcqs.why: AC is the hypotenuse of the right triangle with legs 6 km (east) and 8 km (north): AC = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 km. Halving it gives the equal distance 5 km from the circumcentre to each village.

mcqs.q: It is NOT necessary that a circle passes through every four non-collinear points. A circle passes through four points only when they are:
mcqs.why: A circle will pass through four points only when they are concyclic (lying on one circle). In general, the circle through three of the points does not pass through the fourth, unlike the guaranteed three-point result.

mcqs.q: For a cyclic quadrilateral, the perpendicular bisectors of the sides:
options: Meet at one and the same point O
mcqs.why: For a cyclic quadrilateral the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at one and the same point O, and O is at the same distance from all four vertices. The circle with centre O then passes through all four vertices, and it is the only such circle.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct?
options: All circles are similar, and circles of equal measure are both congruent and similar
Circles are similar only if equal
mcqs.why: Things to remember from the lesson: all circles are always similar. Circles of equal measure (equal radii) are both congruent and similar, while circles of different radii are similar but not congruent.

lessons.title: Exercise 25.2 — Perpendicular from the Centre to a Chord and Length of a Chord
lessons.notes_html:
Diameters Bisect Each Other

Theorem: The diameters of a circle bisect each other.

Proof Step 1: Every diameter passes through the centre of the circle.

Proof Step 2: The centre is the midpoint of every diameter.

Proof Step 3: So the diameters bisect each other at the centre.

Theorem — The Line from the Centre to the Midpoint of a Chord is Perpendicular

Statement: The line drawn from the centre of a circle to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.

In the figure, O is the centre of the circle, AB is a chord, and C is the midpoint of the chord AB. The line OC meets the chord at C.

Proof Step 1: Take the triangles OCA and OCB. OA = OB, because both are radii.
