mcqs.q: If the central angle is θ (in radians) and the radius is r, the length l of the arc is:
mcqs.why: l = rθ. The other forms of the same formula are θ = l/r and r = l/θ. In this formula θ must always be in radians — if the angle is given in degrees, first convert it into radians.

mcqs.q: The area of a sector of radius r and central angle θ (radians) is:
mcqs.why: Area of sector = (1/2)r²θ with θ in radians. For r = 5 cm and θ = π/6 this gives (1/2)(25)(π/6) = 25π/12 ≈ 6.54 cm², the sector half of the lesson's first example.

mcqs.q: If the length of an arc is equal to the radius (l = r), then the angle is:
mcqs.why: From θ = l/r, if l = r then θ = 1 radian — this is the meaning of one radian. Radian measure is defined so that the angle counts how many radius-lengths fit along the arc.

mcqs.q: In a unit circle (r = 1), the arc length is numerically equal to:
options: The angle θ itself: l = θ
mcqs.why: In a unit circle r = 1, so l = rθ becomes l = θ: the arc length equals the angle in radians. For example at 30°, l = π/6 ≈ 0.5236; at 90°, l = π/2 ≈ 1.5708.

mcqs.q: For r = 5 cm and θ = π/6 radian, the arc length is:
mcqs.why: l = rθ = 5 × π/6 = 5π/6 ≈ 2.62 cm. The value 25π/12 ≈ 6.54 cm² is the sector area for the same data — arc (a length) and sector (an area) must not be interchanged.

mcqs.q: For the same data (r = 5 cm, θ = π/6), the area of the sector is:
mcqs.why: Area = (1/2)r²θ = (1/2) × 25 × π/6 = 25π/12 ≈ 6.54 cm². Note the r² in the sector formula: doubling the radius quadruples the sector area but only doubles the arc length.

mcqs.q: A central angle of 84° with radius 12 cm must first be converted to radians:
mcqs.why: θ = 84 × π/180 = 7π/15 radian. Only then can l = rθ be used: l = 12 × 7π/15 = 28π/5 ≈ 17.59 cm — degrees can never be substituted directly into l = rθ.

mcqs.q: For that circle (r = 12 cm, θ = 7π/15), the sector area is:
mcqs.why: Area = (1/2)r²θ = (1/2) × 144 × 7π/15 = 168π/5 ≈ 105.56 cm². The figure 28π/5 ≈ 17.59 is the arc length of the same example, again showing the two formulas side by side.

mcqs.q: A point moving on a circle's circumference covers, in one revolution, a distance of:
mcqs.why: Distance of one revolution = 2πr, the full circumference. For radius 10 cm at 3.5 revolutions per second, the distance in one second is 3.5 × 2π × 10 = 70π ≈ 219.9 cm.

mcqs.q: The relation between angular speed ω and linear speed v is:
mcqs.why: ω = v/r: angular speed is linear speed divided by the radius. Equivalently v = ωr, which is the speed version of the arc formula l = rθ that runs through the whole lesson.

lessons.title: Exercise 30.3 — Coterminal Angles, Quadrants and Values of Special Angles
lessons.notes_html:
Angle in Standard Position

An angle in standard position is one whose vertex is at the origin and whose initial side is the positive part of the x-axis. The quadrant in which the terminal side falls is the quadrant of the angle:

First quadrant: 0° to 90°

Second quadrant: 90° to 180°

Third quadrant: 180° to 270°

Fourth quadrant: 270° to 360°

Coterminal Angles

Angles whose terminal sides are at the same place are coterminal angles. By adding multiples of 360° to a given angle or subtracting them, coterminal angles are obtained:

Coterminal angle = θ + 360°n

Coterminal angle = θ + 2πn (in radians)

Example: The coterminal angles of 55° are 55° + 360° = 415° and 55° - 360° = -305°. In the same way, for -45°: -45° + 360° = 315°.

Signs: Which Ratio is Positive in Which Quadrant?

In the first quadrant all ratios are positive. In the second, only sin and cosec are positive. In the third, only tan and cot are positive. In the fourth, only cos and sec are positive. All the rest are negative.

Examples: 120° is in the second quadrant, so cos 120° is negative. 340° is in the fourth quadrant, so sin 340° is negative. 200° is in the third quadrant, so sec 200° is negative.

Standard Values of Special Angles

These values must be remembered — without them, trigonometry questions cannot be solved:

θ0°30°45°60°90°
sin θ01/21/√2√3/21
cos θ1√3/21/√21/20
tan θ01/√31√3undefined

The remaining ratios are obtained by reciprocals: cosec θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. For example, sec 45° = √2 and cot 45° = 1. In a unit circle, for the point (x, y), sin θ = y and cos θ = x.

Remaining Ratios from One Ratio

Fundamental identity and ratio formulas:

sin²θ + cos²θ = 1

tan θ = sin θ/cos θ

Example: cos θ = -3/5 and θ is in the Second Quadrant — Find the Remaining Ratios

Step 1: In the second quadrant sin is positive and cos is negative.

Step 2: sin²θ = 1 - cos²θ = 1 - 9/25 = 16/25.

Step 3: sin θ = 4/5 (positive, because it is the second quadrant).

Step 4: tan θ = sin θ/cos θ = (4/5)/(-3/5) = -4/3.

Step 5: cot θ = -3/4, sec θ = -5/3, cosec θ = 5/4.

Example: Find the Value of tan 30° tan 60° + tan 45° cot 45°

Step 1: Put the values from the table: tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 60° = √3, tan 45° = 1, cot 45° = 1.

Step 2: Multiply: (1/√3)(√3) = 1 and (1)(1) = 1.

Step 3: Add: 1 + 1 = 2.

mcqs.q: An angle is in standard position when:
options: It lies in the first quadrant
Its terminal side is on the x-axis
Its vertex is at the origin and its initial side is the positive part of the x-axis
mcqs.why: An angle in standard position has its vertex at the origin and its initial side on the positive part of the x-axis. The quadrant in which the terminal side falls is then called the quadrant of the angle.

mcqs.q: Coterminal angles are obtained from θ by:
options: Adding or subtracting multiples of 360°: θ + 360°n
mcqs.why: Coterminal angle = θ + 360°n (or θ + 2πn in radians): angles whose terminal sides are at the same place. Thus 55° has coterminal angles 415° and −305°, and −45° gives 315°.

mcqs.q: The coterminal angles of 55° include:
mcqs.why: 55° + 360° = 415° and 55° − 360° = −305°. Adding or subtracting one full turn returns the terminal side to exactly the same place, which is the definition of coterminal angles.

mcqs.q: In the second quadrant, the positive ratios are:
mcqs.why: First quadrant: all ratios positive. Second: only sin and cosec positive. Third: only tan and cot positive. Fourth: only cos and sec positive; all the rest are negative — the sign chart of the lesson.

mcqs.q: 120° is in the second quadrant, so cos 120° is:
mcqs.why: In the second quadrant only sin and cosec are positive, so cos 120° is negative. Similarly 340° is in the fourth quadrant, so sin 340° is negative, and 200° is in the third, so sec 200° is negative.

mcqs.q: From the special-angles table, sec 45° and cot 45° are:
mcqs.why: The remaining ratios come from reciprocals: sec 45° = 1/cos 45° = 1/(1/√2) = √2, and cot 45° = 1/tan 45° = 1/1 = 1. The table itself gives sin, cos and tan; cosec, sec and cot are their reciprocals.

mcqs.q: In a unit circle, for the point (x, y) on it:
options: sin θ = x and cos θ = y
sin θ = y and cos θ = x
mcqs.why: In a unit circle, sin θ = y and cos θ = x for the point (x, y). This matches the quadrant sign chart: in the second quadrant x is negative, so cos is negative while sin (the y-value) stays positive.

mcqs.q: Given cos θ = −3/5 with θ in the second quadrant, sin θ is:
mcqs.why: sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, and in the second quadrant sin is positive, so sin θ = 4/5. Then tan θ = (4/5)/(−3/5) = −4/3, as the worked example continues.

mcqs.q: For that same angle, tan θ, sec θ and cosec θ are:
mcqs.why: tan θ = sin/cos = −4/3; sec θ = 1/cos θ = −5/3; cosec θ = 1/sin θ = 5/4; and cot θ = −3/4. The signs follow the second-quadrant rule: sin (and cosec) positive, everything else negative.

mcqs.q: The value of tan 30° tan 60° + tan 45° cot 45° is:
mcqs.why: From the table: (1/√3)(√3) + (1)(1) = 1 + 1 = 2. Each product collapses to 1 because tan 30° and tan 60° are reciprocals, and tan 45° = cot 45° = 1.

lessons.title: Exercise 30.4 — Trigonometric Identities
lessons.notes_html:
Fundamental Trigonometric Identities

An identity is an equality which is true for every permissible value of θ. The most important fundamental identities are these:

sin²θ + cos²θ = 1

1 + tan²θ = sec²θ

1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ

tan θ = sin θ/cos θ

cot θ = cos θ/sin θ

Reciprocal relations: sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ and cot θ = 1/tan θ. Many other results come out of these, such as 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ, sec²θ - 1 = tan²θ and cosec θ · sin θ = 1.

Method of Proving an Identity

Take one side — usually the longer side — and by changing it with the fundamental identities, reach the other side. Changing every ratio into sin θ and cos θ is often the easiest way.

Example: Prove sin²θ/cos θ + cos θ = sec θ

Step 1: Take the left side: sin²θ/cos θ + cos θ.

Step 2: Bring it to the common denominator cos θ: (sin²θ + cos²θ)/cos θ.

Step 3: Use the fundamental identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1: 1/cos θ.

Step 4: 1/cos θ = sec θ = right side. Proved.

Example: Prove cos⁴θ - sin⁴θ = cos²θ - sin²θ

Step 1: Factorize the left side: (cos²θ - sin²θ)(cos²θ + sin²θ).

Step 2: cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, so the left side = (cos²θ - sin²θ) × 1.

Step 3: = cos²θ - sin²θ = right side. Proved.

Example: Change (sec θ + 1)(sec θ - 1) into tan²θ

Step 1: By the form (a + 1)(a - 1) = a² - 1: (sec θ + 1)(sec θ - 1) = sec²θ - 1.

Step 2: From the identity 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, sec²θ - 1 = tan²θ.

Step 3: Answer: (sec θ + 1)(sec θ - 1) = tan²θ.

Other proved results: (1 + sin θ)/cos θ = tan θ + sec θ, because tan θ + sec θ = sin θ/cos θ + 1/cos θ = (1 + sin θ)/cos θ; and cosec θ + cot θ = (1 + cos θ)/sin θ, because cosec θ + cot θ = 1/sin θ + cos θ/sin θ.

mcqs.q: The fundamental identity of trigonometry is:
mcqs.why: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every angle θ. The other two identities of the lesson, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ, are derived from it by division.

mcqs.q: Dividing sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 throughout by cos²θ gives:
mcqs.why: Dividing by cos²θ: sin²θ/cos²θ + 1 = 1/cos²θ, that is, tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ. Dividing instead by sin²θ gives the third identity, 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

mcqs.q: If sin θ = 3/5 (θ acute), then cos θ is:
mcqs.why: From sin²θ + cos²θ = 1: cos²θ = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, so cos θ = 4/5 (positive, since θ is acute). This 3-4-5 pattern is exactly the worked example with sec θ = 3/√5 in the notes.

mcqs.q: 1 + cot²θ equals:
mcqs.why: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ, obtained by dividing the fundamental identity by sin²θ. Together with tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ, these are the three identities proved in this lesson.

mcqs.q: If cos θ = 12/13, then sin θ (θ acute) is:
mcqs.why: sin²θ = 1 − 144/169 = 25/169, so sin θ = 5/13 for acute θ. The 5-12-13 triple appears because the identity is Pythagoras in disguise — the same arithmetic as the circle examples.

mcqs.q: sec²θ − tan²θ equals:
mcqs.why: From 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, moving tan²θ across gives sec²θ − tan²θ = 1. Rearranged forms like this are the everyday use of the identities in simplification questions.

mcqs.q: In the worked example, with the given ratio the value sec θ comes out as:
mcqs.why: The notes' example finds sec θ = 3/√5 by first getting the remaining ratio from sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 and then taking the reciprocal for sec. Identity first, reciprocal second — the standard two-step.

mcqs.q: cosec²θ − cot²θ equals:
mcqs.why: From 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ we get cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1. Each of the three identities rearranges to a difference of squares equal to 1 in this way.

mcqs.q: The identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 holds:
mcqs.why: The fundamental identity holds for every angle θ — it is not restricted to the special angles of the table or to acute angles. The derived identities need only that the denominators (cos θ or sin θ) are not zero.

mcqs.q: If tan θ = 4/3 (θ acute), then sec θ is:
mcqs.why: sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ = 1 + 16/9 = 25/9, so sec θ = 5/3 for acute θ. No triangle needs to be drawn: the second identity gives sec directly from tan.

lessons.title: Exercise 30.5 — Angles of Elevation and Depression: Questions of Height and Distance
lessons.notes_html:
Angle of Elevation and Angle of Depression

If an object is above the level of the observer, the angle between the horizontal ray and the line of sight is called the angle of elevation. If the object is below, that angle is called the angle of depression.

Remember: The angle of depression of an object below from a top is equal to the angle of elevation of the top from that object (alternate angles). So a question of the angle of depression is changed into the angle of elevation and solved with a right triangle.

Method: Which Ratio to Use?

In a right triangle, for the angle θ:

tan θ = opposite side (perpendicular) / adjacent side (base)

sin θ = opposite side / hypotenuse

If height and horizontal distance are given, use tan; if height and the sloping length (such as a ladder) are given, use sin.

Example: Distance of a Ship from a 102m High Lighthouse (Angle of Depression 30°18′)

Step 1: Angle of depression = angle of elevation from the ship = 30°18′ = 30.3°.

Step 2: Suppose the horizontal distance of the ship from the lighthouse is x. In the triangle, tan(30.3°) = 102/x.

Step 3: Take tan(30.3°) ≈ 0.5843.

Step 4: x = 102/0.5843 ≈ 174.6m.

Step 5: Answer: The ship is about 174.6m away from the lighthouse.

Example: Length of a Ladder (Angle 60° with the Ground, Height 6m)

Step 1: The ladder is the hypotenuse; suppose its length is L.

Step 2: sin 60° = 6/L, because the opposite side is 6m.

Step 3: sin 60° = √3/2, so L = 6/(√3/2) = 12/√3 = 4√3.

Step 4: Answer: L ≈ 6.93m.

Example: Height of a Hill (Angle 30°, then 45° after Going 210m Closer)

Step 1: Suppose the height is h and the distance from the nearer point is x.

Step 2: tan 45° = h/x, and tan 45° = 1, so x = h.

Step 3: From the farther point, tan 30° = h/(x + 210), that is, 1/√3 = h/(h + 210).

Step 4: From this, h + 210 = h√3, that is, 210 = h(√3 - 1).

Step 5: h = 210/(√3 - 1) = 105(√3 + 1) ≈ 286.9m.

Another Example: Shadow of a Bamboo and the Angle

If the shadow of a 6m high bamboo is 2√3m, then tan θ = 6/(2√3) = √3, so the angle of elevation θ = 60°. In the same way, the angle of depression of a farmhouse at a horizontal distance of 9613m from an observer 4280m above: tan θ = 4280/9613 ≈ 0.4452, so θ ≈ 24°.

mcqs.q: The angle of elevation is measured:
options: Upward from the horizontal to the line of sight
mcqs.why: The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight, measured upward when the object is above the observer. Looking down instead gives the angle of depression.

mcqs.q: The angle of depression is measured:
options: Downward from the horizontal to the line of sight
mcqs.why: The angle of depression is between the horizontal and the line of sight, measured downward, when the object is below the observer's level. Elevation and depression are both measured from the horizontal, never from the vertical.

mcqs.q: A pole's top is seen at an elevation of 60° from a point 10 m from its foot. The pole's height is:
mcqs.why: tan 60° = height/10, so height = 10 × tan 60° = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m. The height is the side opposite the angle and the distance is the adjacent side, making tan the right ratio.

mcqs.q: From the top of a 20 m building, a car on the ground is seen at a depression of 30°. The car's distance from the foot is:
mcqs.why: By alternate angles, the angle inside the triangle at the car is also 30°, and tan 30° = 20/distance, so distance = 20/tan 30° = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m. Depression problems convert to an ordinary right triangle this way.

mcqs.q: The angle of depression from the top equals:
options: The angle of elevation from the object looking up (alternate angles)
mcqs.why: The angle of depression from the top of an object equals the angle of elevation from the object on the ground, by alternate angles between the parallel horizontal lines. This equality is what makes depression problems solvable as ordinary triangles.

mcqs.q: An observer sees a tower's top at elevation 45° from 50 m away. The tower's height is:
mcqs.why: tan 45° = height/50 and tan 45° = 1, so height = 50 × 1 = 50 m. At 45° the height and the distance are always equal — a quick check for such problems.

mcqs.q: A kite's string is 40 m long and makes an angle of 60° with the horizontal. The kite's height above the ground is:
mcqs.why: Here the string is the hypotenuse: height = 40 × sin 60° = 40 × (√3/2) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m. Sin is used because the known side is the hypotenuse rather than the adjacent — ratio choice depends on which sides are involved.

mcqs.q: Which ratio is used when the known side is the hypotenuse and the wanted side is opposite the angle?
mcqs.why: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, so sin connects the opposite side with the hypotenuse. If instead the adjacent side and hypotenuse are involved, cos is the ratio to use.

mcqs.q: The 'line of sight' is:
options: The line joining the observer's eye to the object
mcqs.why: The line of sight joins the observer's eye to the object being viewed. The angle of elevation or depression is the angle between this line and the horizontal through the eye.

mcqs.q: From a point, the elevation of a building's top is 30° and the distance is 30√3 m. The building's height is:
mcqs.why: height = distance × tan 30° = 30√3 × (1/√3) = 30 m. The √3 cancels neatly — a sign the numbers were chosen from the special-angle table, as in the chapter's examples.
